Local banks’ appetite may have hit a ceiling: Local demand has been a very supportive factor for ILGOVs in recent years (Figure 7), as the burden of absorbing the additional issuance has fallen primarily on domestic investors. Local banks’ allocation to domestic debt seems to have found a ceiling at relatively high levels (Figure 8). With a stable loan-to-deposit ratio of around 75%, assuming deposit growth at 5% (in line with GDP) and their allocation to domestic debt falling slightly to 8%, demand for ILGOVs from the domestic banking system should be essentially flat this year, in our view. Local institutional demand will remain supported: Where we see scope for strong demand to continue is from local institutional investors. The public’s (households and firms) financial assets portfolio continues to grow at a rate close to 15% y/y. The allocation to domestic debt has also risen (Figure 8), as repatriation flows remain a key theme in Israel. Assuming the public’s portfolio grows by 12% in 2026 and allocation to domestic government debt remains at 7%, local demand should comfortably exceed ILS50bn, more than enough to absorb this year’s net issuance. As such, meaningfully tighter ASWs will likely require a rise in foreign positioning, we would argue. The demand for reserves under this scarce framework was also very straightforward for the Fed to determine. The Fed would calculate the reserve requirement for each individual bank based on deposit levels. So, it had a clearly defined demand curve in aggregate. Today, the bank reserve demand curve is a function of many more factors and is harder to define with much precision outside of observation in real time. Banks also tend to hold reserves in excess of what is their least comfortable level, and demand is also quite non-linear as the level approaches scarcity, as evidenced by the funding crisis of 2019 sparked by Fed QT . All of this is to say that should the Fed end RMPs, let alone restart QT , we would likely start to observe emerging funding market pressures in short order ( Figure 2). GERMANY: GOVERNMENT COLLAPSE Why it’s important: The German growth revival is the centrepiece of the ‘make Europe Great Again’ story. Markets are pricing a growth recovery in Germany and the eurozone, with more German borrowing and an increase in pan- European defence spending. The growth story also underpins the increase in inflation in our forecast that results in hikes from the ECB in H2 2027. How it might happen: GDP growth is zero in H1 and there are negative European corporate guidance revisions. The AfD obtains more than 25% of seats in both March state elections and enters state-level government after the September state elections. Against this backdrop, the pension reform vote fails, triggering a vote of no-confidence, which passes, and the government collapses. Our bullish USDJPY view is based on domestic and global factors. On the domestic front, the new administration’s expansionary fiscal policies and dovish monetary policy bias should continue to weigh on the currency, while verbal interventions so far indicate that any eventual action may still be steps away. In addition, the JPY may face further selling pressures due to its correlation to the JGB term premia, particularly if Takaichi decides to call for an early snap election that strengthens her political mandate to pursue more expansionary economic policies (see the JPY part of the overview). The limits of federal action It is important to note that, absent accompanying measures to increase supply, measures that boost demand—such as lower mortgage rates or down payment assistance—tend to push prices higher over time, making them an unsustainable solu- tion for long-term affordability. Given these dynamics, the fact that a large body of academic evidence indicates local zoning and permitting regulations—not federal policy—are the primary barriers to new housing supply (Glaeser and Gyourko, 2003, 2025; Gyourko and Molloy, 2015) suggests that federal action alone cannot resolve the problem. Congress is advancing bipartisan legislation on this front. Both chambers have now passed major housing bills—the Senate’s ROAD to Housing Act and the House’s newly passed Housing in the 21st Century Act—which are now headed for reconciliation. Both bills aim to ramp up incen- tives for local governments to reform restrictive zoning and permitting practices in undersupplied markets. After all the details are hammered out and a final bill becomes law, the effectiveness of these measures will be challenged by a reli- ance on local governments to respond to these incentives. Most of the provisions in these bills simply expand on exist- ing programs and are unlikely to fully resolve the structural barriers at the heart of the affordability issue. THEME OF THE WEEK: A TOUGH(ER) ACT TO FOLLOW Both 2024 and 2025 saw wholesale interest rate easing across EM central banks (an average of five EM rate cuts per month across each year). January 2026 has seen a different narrative take hold with a Colombia rate hike and looser policy in Israel and Turk ey only. One month does not make a trend – and not all central banks have monthly policy announcement cadences – but it does likely suggest a more muted outlook for rates. Part of that is driven by cyclical cumulative easing, part related to fiscal fears, and part concerned around rate differentials. As highlighted on page 3, opportunities still exist, but returns across carry, duration and currency last year suggest that the low hanging fruit in EM rates has been reaped. A more opportunistic 2026 awaits in the asset class. EC considers increasing SAFE - EU bond supply to stay high after 2027 According to Bloomberg, "the EU is exploring possibilities for fresh defense funding after an initial EUR 150bn loan program was oversubscribed. The "discussions are in the early stages." The European Commission (EC) is currently working on disbursements under the already existing loan programme. In our view, the EC considering further possibilities for defence funding is hardly surprising. We struggle to see EU bond supply to drop significantly after 2026 and 2027 because the EC continues to consider/propose more common EU debt due to different reasons, for example, defence , reconstruction of Ukraine after the war and the up to EUR 400bn crisis mechanism under the next 7y EU budget. While the usual challenges in the EU Council likely persists (i.e. preference for loans instead of grants by so-called frugal MS), annual EU bond supply of around EUR 160bn could still be on the horizon also after 2027. The likely high EU bond supply also going forward is the main reason why we typically struggle to be very bullish on spreads of EU bonds - despite the extremely strong legal support mechanism stipulated in EU laws and strong political support by EU MS (for example, also Germany) and the attractive pick-up (for example, versus EIB and KfW). records.text: ab 13 February 2026 Global Research Global Rates Strategy Weekly Supply: Buying duration before St. Valentine Decent duration bid this week If syndications from EGB issuers were concentrated in the 10y–20y segment in January, issuance is now extending further out the curve in February, notably into the 30y sector. This week, France completed a stellar 30y OAT syndication: with record order books of around €135bn, the AFT placed €8bn of the new OAT 2057. Earlier this month, Belgium also launched a new 30y OLO, again attracting a record order book, with demand more than twice that seen for the 30y issued in 2025. In January, Italy’s Tesoro syndicated a new 15y BTP to market, issuing a record €14bn in a single transaction—the largest ever in this segment by an EGB issuer. Looking ahead, we expect Spain’s Tesoro could explore the 30y segment in the coming weeks. Strong demand across the EGB duration spectrum should give Spain greater confidence to do so. A steeper curve and relatively low volatility across the EUR rates curve should continue to support demand at the long end. We also expect two 30y syndications from Germany this year, with the first potentially as early as March. It is no exaggeration to say that EM currencies are often hostage to global conditions and broader risk appetite. This is not to underestimate the impact of idiosyncratic factors and relative macro/policy direction. However, a more generic view on EM is often a function of factors beyond the asset class. One such factor is the impact of the USD . EM are, in effect, the mirror image of USD directionality and USD performance is highly negatively correlated with EM assets (Figure 2). Although USD real money positioning remains underweight, the combination of diversification/hedging prospects, Fed easing bias and valuations should continue to put the USD under pressure. Exposure to commodity currencies and high yielding EM assets continue to make sense against that backdrop despite a stronger December NFP prin t in the US – a modest impact on Fed rate expectations – and a more balanced view around overall risk appetite. records.text: ny months away. With politics quietening down, we think OATs should continue to enjoy a TINA (there is no alternative) dynamic. For any EUR-denominated investor, the French debt market offers depth and liquidity with a reasonable rating (A+), which few other similarly rated euro area sovereigns provide. Hence, while there remain significant structural challenges for French bonds (fiscal/ political), for the market to punish OATs a catalyst would be needed, especially given the current low-volatility carry-hunting backdrop. Absent that catalyst (eg, political turbulence), the 'honeymoon bliss' that OATs are enjoying should last, in our view. In our 2026 outlook, we had pencilled in a range for OAT-Bund of 65-100bp; given recent developments, we have revised this range to 50-95bp. For the remainder of H1, we think the path of least resistance would be for OAT-Bund to trade resiliently towards the lower end of this range, especially given supportive demand dynamics for several key investor segments, as we discuss below. We think French spreads will only be likely to move towards the upper end of our 2026 trading range in H2 if political turbulence re-emerges as the 2027 budget-setting process gets under way. records.text: Doubts around fiscal prudence: In September 2022, the UK government, under the leadership of Prime Minister Liz Truss, announced GBP45bn of unfunded tax cuts. The so-called mini-budget led to a 120bp surge in gilt yields in a week and a nearly 3% decline in the GBP (Figure 1). Though the policy decisions were ultimately reversed, the damage remained, and UK assets have stayed sensitive to any signs of fiscal distress globally. Since then, fiscal consolidation efforts and a renewed government commitment to fiscal prudence have softened the impact. However, over three years later, risks are brewing again, due to divisions within Labour and a shift in the political environment away from legacy parties and towards Reform UK and the Greens (Figure 2), which advocate either further tax cuts or more generous public services. Accordingly, we consider a ‘grey swan’ scenario of GBP45bn of additional, unfunded policy measures to increase welfare and administrative spending (e.g. on income support programmes, NHS and other departmental spending, public-sector pay rises, nationalisation), which we see resulting in a short-lived shock and a resurgence of UK risk premium on credibility concerns. 28 Fig. 1: There was a significant reaction in UK assets in the immediate aftermath of the September 2022 mini-budget, with sensitivity since then to fiscal news Sources: Bank of England, Macrobond, BNP Paribas Fig. 2: UK voting intentions show that there has been a significant shift in the politica

records.text: Global Commodities 13 February 2026 Citi Research 4 Longer-term a relaxation of the EU ETS through 2040 would delay the time when physical emission cuts, through capex investments, would be needed. Therefore, as EUAs’ valuation should be the indifference costs between buying EUAs as a way for compliance entities to comply vs. the discounted to present value physical cuts to emissions through installations of emission abatement methods, for instance via CCUS for cement, or changes to energy sourcing, for instance from gas to electrification through renewables, then pushing the time when physical compliance is needed would increase the number of years of discounting, thereby lowering EUA fair value prices. In terms of time frame, the additional supply through the Flexibility Share leftover could occur via a Delegate Act, while the others would likely need to go through the Ordinary Legislative Procedure. Generally, the former is faster, requiring between 6-12 months, from the political decision to publication, with entry into force typically the following year, with the EU Commission adopting it after a technical consultation and the EU Parliament and the EU Council left to only scrutinize the act, without the possibility to rewrite it; instead, the latter is longer, between 18-36 months. records.text: 9 Fig. 6: Valuation of equities versus rates US TREASURIES: 30Y YIELDS EXCEED 6% Fig. 5: Stylized depiction of US Treasury yields after a hypothetical Treasury tantrum Source: BNP Paribas 12/02/2026 Most exposed: Almost every asset class Guneet Dhingra, Head of US Rates Strategy | BNP Paribas Securities Corp. The epicenter of all financial valuations: Treasuries hold a unique place in the global financial system as a ‘risk-free’ asset. Consequently, all risky assets – including but not exclusively equities, credit, commodities, and cryptocurrencies – draw from the valuation of the risk-free rates (real and nominal). For a start, US Treasuries are typically decomposed into rate expectations and term premiums, whereas other credit bonds are rated with an additional component of ‘credit risk’. If a Treasury tantrum pushed 30y yields to 6% or higher, bringing the risk-free status of US Treasuries into question, Treasury yields could also start trading with a new “credit-risk premium”. That means Treasury yields could be structurally higher after such an episode (see Figure 5 for a stylized example). As yields move structurally higher, it would also threaten the valuations of risky assets such as credit and equities, not only because Treasury yields are an input to most valuation models, but also because, on a fundamental level, higher yields could negatively affect growth and worsen fundamentals for the economy. records.text: Option 1: Shrinking the balance sheet Given Warsh's criticism of the size of the balance sheet, he may consider status quo policies unsatisfactory. Needless to say, he would need to have the FOMC on board to effect any changes. Figure 1 shows what happens if the Fed reduces RMPs to zero starting January 2027 to keep the balance sheet constant in USD terms. Reserves, over time, fall in USD terms as non-reserve liabilities continue to grow. As a share of bank assets, they fall to 8-9%. In terms of the composition, Treasuries would account for 75% of all assets, T-bills as share of all Treasuries would rise to about 25%, and the WAM of the Treasury portfolio would fall to about 7 years. We think this strategy presents risks, and the Fed may find it difficult to reduce reserve balances while staying within its "ample" framework. But what is ample? The Fed defines "ample" as a framework where it provides enough reserves to the banking system such that the Fed does not need to actively manage the level of reserves on a day-to-day basis, and the level of the policy rate is set using administered rates. In a sense, this allows banks to largely hold their desired level of reserves without facing a significant trade-off to other short-duration assets. Reserve demand under the current system is driven by banks' internal liquidity needs, their desired mix of HQLA under LCR rules, and a consideration for net stable funding needs. records.text: 10 Global Economic Weekly | 13 February 2026 Disinflation is a sign of economic weakness; risks are firmly to the downside Disinflation in France has probably helped to preserve economic activity (or employment) in level terms. It was surprising to us that the economy has manoeuvred the economic policy uncertainty shock from the 2024 snap elections quite so well (Exhibit 13). Partially, external price competitiveness may have helped to buffer the potential effects on the economy via domestic demand, although the EUR appreciation of 2025 and the EURUSD appreciation at the beginning of this year tone down the effect. But to a larger extent, fiscal policy may have come to the rescue, albeit accidentally. Don’t get us wrong: the 2023 fiscal slippage and its lasting deterioration on the forward looking deficit trajectory meaningfully weighs on our otherwise still benign structural view on France. But swift disinflation means higher short- and long-term real interest rates in France than elsewhere in the Euro area, relatively speaking. Fiscal policy may have accidentally helped to avoid worse growth outcomes for the wrong reasons. Looking forward, that creates all kinds of fragility, and generally a risk balance to both growth and inflation that is firmly tilted to the downside, perhaps even more so than in the Euro area as a whole. records.text: 4 Global FX weekly | 13 February 2026 The view Claudio Piron Merrill Lynch (Singapore) claudio.piron@bofa.com Adarsh Sinha Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) adarsh.sinha@bofa.com G10 FX: the upside down Two unusual episodes in G10 FX markets stood out this week: a muted USD response to strong jobs data and a sizeable JPY rally following the LDP’s election sweep. We draw more signal from USD’s apathy than JPY’s outsized reaction. Risk premium & rest of the world outweighs strong US data The strong US jobs report barely registered a USD response. The usual suspect of positioning doesn’t pass muster as the market was clearly leaning towards a weak print. In fact, this extends a period of USD underperformance vs. relative data surprises since the beginning of 2026 (Exhibit 5). Rising US risk premium partly explains this, but so does the other side of the coin – the outlook for the rest of the world. German factory orders, a potential US-China deal in April and Japan’s election result all bode well for growth in the next biggest economies, even if not immediately evident in the data. While US growth will likely remain solid in 1H, especially around the peak tax refund season from Feb-April, we expect it to decelerate in 2H just as sequential growth elsewhere improves. FX (and relative equity) performance is consistent with markets looking beyond the near-term divergence in data surprises. Both 1929 and 1999 exhibited very fat left tails. But in terms of volatility, they had little in common. When the bubble popped in 1929, our model VIX peaked at about 100, one of the most violent spikes in US equity history. In contrast, the 1999 burst was one of the lowest-velocity bear markets on record: the NDX halved before 9/11 without VIX exceeding 35. Equity bear markets tend to be much longer and deeper during economic recessions. But the most convex crashes are typically a function of leverage and positioning, rather than fundamentals. We think a tech crash scenario could result in both, with the first signs driving a volatile unwind of investor leverage followed by a sustained, deep US equity market drawdown. US equity market structure has evolved in recent years to foster an environment of excess risk-taking vulnerable to swift reversion during exogenous shocks. The epicenter of this exuberance is in the global-semis ETF SMH, whose biggest weights are at the core of the AI story. Private credit has grown faster than public this cycle, with an outsized share for software sector: Historically, the sectors with the strongest debt growth in credit cycles were responsible for subsequent problems (e.g. telecoms in the late 1990s, financials in 2007, energy in 2016). In the current cycle, US private credit growth of 90% (versus five years ago) has materially outpaced US HY (20%) and US LL (27%). US private credit AUM reached USD1trn in 2025, approaching the size of the US HY and LL markets at USD1.4trn and USD1.5trn respectively. Using BDCs as a proxy, business services and software comprise 20% and 18%, respectively. Sticky MTM valuations in private credit do not show signs of fundamental deterioration: The illiquid nature of private credit debt is a source of vulnerability to the market. Private credit loans are still lagging in terms of pricing efficiency, given limited secondary trading. This is reflected by the flat nature of NAV in most BDCs, which have remained unchanged over the last few quarterly reporting dates. This is in contrast with public markets, which have been more reactive in repricing risks related to private credit, either directly (public BDC share prices) or indirectly (‘CCC’ leveraged loans, see Figure 2). The gilt market is benefiting from a de-escalation in near-term political risk, although it could hang over the market for some time, with volatility likely around known political flash points in the coming months. Next week’s data round may turn the focus back onto MPC pricing. The market is heavily skewed towards a March cut creating the risk-reward to position for April instead, in our view. A political timeline for gilt volatility The market is rewarding near-term political stability over longer-term fiscal vulnerability. The evidence is the 13bp tightening in 10yr OAT-Bunds (to 59bp, 16:45 GMT 12Feb26) so far this year and the 13bp rally in 30yr JGBs (to 3.41% close 12Feb25) since last weekend’s election in Japan. The volatility in gilts since last Wednesday offers another example. While 10yr yields are now 7bp lower over the period (currently 4.45%, 16:45 GMT 12Feb26) there were a couple of intra-day spikes to 4.6% when Prime Minister Starmer appeared at his most vulnerable. A political timeline for gilt volatility. What happens next is still hard to predict, but our base case is unchanged from a week ago in that any challenge is still most likely after May, perhaps in the run up to the Labour Conference on 27-30 September. While in aggregate delinquencies have returned to their pre pandemic norm, there are clear bifurcations at the sector level. Products typically associated with lower-income consumers such as credit card lending or personal loans (bucketed into the “other” category in FRBNY data) have accounted for far more than their fair share of the increase in delinquent dollars and are well above their pre-pandemic norms. Credit cards are responsible for 25% of the increase in delinquent dollars while they make up less than 7% of total consumer debt at the present. The “other” category is responsible for 5% of the increase in delinquent dollars while loans in this sector account for only 3% of consumer lending more broadly. While auto lending delinquencies have increased largely in line with aggregate delinquencies since year-end 2022, they started in a worse relative position than other lending types. D90+ rates within the sector sit near their highest levels on record. Lending products catering to more affluent borrowers (namely mortgages and home equity products) have seen small increases in delinquent balances since year-end 2022 and remain near the low end of their historical range, likely supported by borrowers locking in low rates during the pandemic as well as building up large amounts of equity over the last several years. Much of the administration’s rhetoric on demand-side interventions has focused on lowering mortgage rates, which remain elevated relative to both the historic lows seen during the pandemic and the previous decade’s average. As our glob- al team recently highlighted, the US stands out among DM economies in that higher mortgage rates have done little to bring down prices. Elevated borrowing costs have reinforced “lock‑in” among owners, keeping resale inventory tight. The president has already directed the GSEs (Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac) to purchase $200bn in mortgage-backed securi- ties. This directive began with purchases of $16bn per month, which if sustained would reach the target in just under a year. The spread of the primary mortgage rate to the 10-year Trea- sury rate tightened by roughly 10bp on the announcement. For reference, the Fed’s third round of QE in 2012 involved $40bn per month of MBS purchases and led to a short-lived 50bp tightening in spreads. A tightening of that magnitude is unlikely here, as the GSEs lack the firepower of the Fed and must manage balance sheet risk and potential losses. The administration may consider encouraging the Fed to redi- rect MBS runoff back into MBS to further tighten spreads. Outside capital asset appreciation (in Taiwanese equities and real estate), there is no strong evidence that the gains from the AI‑export boom have meaningfully spilled over to the non‑tech parts of the economy and to the median Taiwanese worker. The K-shaped economy leaves the CBC in a hard place The strong K‑shaped economy leaves the CBC in a hard place. Strong nominal and real GDP growth prevents the CBC from being dovish. However, both headline and core CPI remain below target, and the narrow gains from the AI‑export boom prevent the CBC from turning hawkish. We see the more likely course for the CBC to traverse in this divergent policy landscape is to remain on hold and watch for signs of whether the benefits from the AI‑export boom are spilling over into stronger consumption and higher realized inflation. As such, we think the current CBC path priced by Taiwan’s interest rate swap curve of three hikes over the next 12 months remains aggressive and is something that should be faded. Moreover, with the changes in regulation on Taiwanese lifers regarding the recognition of FX losses and FX hedging, we think the threshold for the CBC to hike will likely have increased further relative to the past.

records.text: Carlin Doyle 13 February 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Over the Hedge A shake up is occurring in EM FX hedging behaviour. Hedge ratios for EM LC bonds have dropped, in aggregate, back to the long-term average. In part, this is a result of low -hedged inflows into Brazilian bonds as well as a reassessment of global risk. Despite headline grabbing drops in stocks and gold , as well as geopolitical events, fear is falling. This is largely due to confirmation that global trade remains robust. Excessive hedging activity, which took off on Liberation Day, is now finally correcting. In addition, EM interest rates are lowering which is historically associated with reduced risk. Investor sentiment is finally, after more than a year into Trump’s second presidency, returning to normal. The hedging behaviour of institutional investors towards EM LC debt is shifting dramatically. Since the start of 2026, the aggregate measure of investors ’ FX hedging of underlying fixed income has moved from excessive, back in line with the long -run average (Figure 1). That this move has happened at all, is something of a surprise given this year has seen two seismic geopolitical events and a reassessment of both Tech stocks and gold prices. As far as EM investors are concerned, the lowering of hedge ratios suggest that the global investment climate has become more attractive, not less. In other February commu- nications, the leadership identified rising domestic demand as the primary driver of inflation. Governor Bullock reinforced this view in recent parliamentary hearings, stating that demand is "too high" relative to the economy's supply capaci- ty. This implies that the RBA may need to tighten further and that growth may need to be sacrificed to contain inflation. The RBA's firm messaging appears at odds with lingering uncertainty around the degree of inflation persistence. Last year, the RBA incorporated nuances in inflation performance, including the role of global and government policy-related factors in contrast to those driven through the labor market. The February SoMP highlighted that the bank still views the most recent increase in inflation as mostly temporary, but hiked anyway. This suggests reduced patience for further inflation overshoots and perhaps more of a risk management bias on inflation, as opposed to growth/labor market. In our view, given that the ESM is fully up and running, has plenty of unused lending capacity, a solid triple A rating by five rating agencies (Moody's, S&P, Fitch, DBRS, Scope), we think using the ESM for defence lending would be an easy and very elegant solution. However, the ESM is a crisis-resolution mechanism for countries in the euro area, established as an intergovernmental organization under public international law by a treaty that entered into force on Sept 27, 2012 without direct involvement of the European Commission (EC). Hence, we still doubt that defence lending will become the new main purpose of the ESM. The EC will likely prefer other options, for example, an increase of SAFE. Accordingly, we expect spreads of the ESM to stay at the tight end of the EUR SSA space, supported by relatively low supply and the extremely strong credit quality. If we are wrong and defence lending becomes a topic for the ESM, we think making significant use of the unused lending capacity would still be unlikely as this might be targeted for smaller euro area countries. Only in the event this becomes a major topic of the ESM, making significant use of its unused lending capacity, current spreads seem too tight at current levels. records.text: Agency MBS FHFA provides GSEs with greater flexibility to purchase MBS; however, the PSP A-imposed portfolio cap is not relaxed yet The annual reports filed by the GSEs earlier this week provide additional insights into their retained portfolios with important implications for the agency MBS market. As of December 2025, the sizes of Fannie and Freddie’s investment portfolios were $132.5 billion and $139.2 billion, respectively. Single-family MBS accounted for $70.4 billion and $40.2 billion, respectively, an increase of $30 billion and $19 billion year over year (Exhibit 1). In a social media post on January 23rd, Director Pulte noted that the FHFA provided GSEs legal flexibility to go beyond their existing caps. However, it appears that the PSPA-related portfolio cap of $225 billion has not been revised yet. Rather, FHFA has removed the additional portfolio restrictions they imposed on GSE portfolios, such as the $40 billion cap on single-family MBS and the requirement to maintain the size of the portfolio below 90% of the PSPA-imposed cap. As a result, GSEs can now buy agency MBS until their portfolio size hits $225 billion. This is especially important for investors focused on the valuation case for a weaker Dollar. Based on our GSDEER and GSFEER models, the Dollar’s overvaluation is now entirely attributable to currencies in Asia (especially CNY and JPY) (Exhibit 1). AUD: Let me love you. Despite the recent hit to its terms of trade from the selloff in n metals, the AUD has continued to strengthen through our 12-month forecast, supported by the RBA delivering the first hike by a major central bank. We think this dynamic can continue, especially as AUD still remains about 2 percentage points below GSBEER-implied performance over the past 6 months. In this scenario, 10y gilt yields could rise by more than 55bp and the GBP could weaken by 4%, displaying a comparable relationship between gilts and the GBP that has become increasingly close in the recent years ever since the 2022 mini- budget crisis. Higher rates, driven by fiscal risk premia: On top of the market’s reassessment of inflation and BoE policy, longer-dated gilts would also be under pressure as the market reprices higher fiscal risk premium. Our 5y5y term premia model shows a 85bp upward impact on the 5y5y (to about 5.95%), and our 10y gilt expectations model shows that the upwards jump in risk premia would translate into a more than 55bp jump in 10y gilt yields. That said, our analysis suggests that the propensity for the market to sell off in this scenario, while potentially meaningful, would be more limited than the 2022 mini-budget crisis. by 75% and 77%, respectively, in 2024 and 2025, our equity analysts' prior forecast had Hyperscaler capex slowing to annual growth rates of 39% and 16% in 2026 and 2027. Now, their forecasts assume annual growth of 65% and 22%. Still a slowdown, but much less pronounced in terms of growth rates in 2026. The sharper slowdown is pushed out a year into 2027. Their revised estimates have implications for our outlook for nonresidential business fixed investment, since AI-related capex spending shows through in equipment spending (computers and peripherals), intellectual property investment (software), and structures (data and power centers). However, as we noted in previous research reports (see here and here), capex spending announcements are different than GDP-based accounting. Hyperscaler capex spending that goes to purchases of intermediate goods are not included in GDP, which captures final output, and spending in categories like computers and peripherals has high import content, which is netted out of GDP calculations since it focuses on domestic product.

records.text: That said, we expect the economies to look more similar this year along several dimensions. First, we expect growth to pick up in both economies (Exhibit 2). We forecast UK growth of 1.4% on a Q4/Q4 basis in 2026 (up from 1% last year) with US growth edging up to 2.5% (above last year’s 2.3%). Easing financial conditions, receding trade tensions and falling inflation play key roles in supporting growth. Consistent with this, the monthly activity data have improved across the Atlantic, with our Current Activity Indicators picking up notably into 2026. Second, both labour markets look soft (Exhibit 3). The UK jobless rate has risen by 1½pp since the 2022 low and almost 1pp over the last year, standing clearly above its structural rate. The US unemployment rate has risen less during this period—and has recently edged down—but the jobs market likewise has spare capacity (especially when broader slack indicators are taken into account). Looking at OIS pricing, even after the election – and despite the correction in JPY weakness – the probability of a rate hike by the April meeting has remained stable at slightly less than 80%. This suggests that rate‑hike expectations themselves may be one factor contributing to the correction in JPY depreciation. In addition, broadly consistent with our forecast, markets are pricing in almost two rate hikes by the October meeting. That said, if USDJPY were to fall well below 150, early rate hikes could become less likely. As such, close attention will need to be paid to FX developments and the BoJ’s messaging in response. We see two-way risks to our April rate hike outlook. If JPY depreciation pressure resumes and intervention becomes difficult, a rate hike at the March meeting cannot be ruled out. Conversely, if China‑related risks stemming from PM Takaichi’s comments on a potential Taiwan contingency become pronounced, the BoJ could be pushed to downgrade its economic or inflation outlook or its risk balance in the April Outlook Report, increasing the chances of a wait‑and‑see stance. We look at options the Fed has for reducing its footprint and, importantly, how Treasury may adjust its issuance strategy. The outlook for the Fed’s balance sheet continues to occupy investors' attention, and the topic is starting to be reflected in public remarks from Fed speakers this week. We have argued that there seems to be a cohort at the Fed that, despite the Fed initiating reserve management purchases (RMPs ) and growing its securities portfolio, wishes to end up with a “smaller” balance sheet down the road. This was evident in the December meeting minutes, and we think Kevin Warsh’s nomination as Fed chair puts potentially greater emphasis on this front, given his views on the subject (see here). For instance, comments from KC Fed President Schmid were clearly tilted to the hawkish side on balance sheet policy this week, even while supporting the Fed’s actions taken in December to grow system liquidity. Flows from levered ETFs, retail investors, CTAs, and volatility target funds create a complex and potentially volatile mixture in US equities (see US EQD: Buy the dip in spot and vol, dated 3 January). Recessionary reaction: We see a risk of the first signs of a tech crash driving a convex unwind of investor leverage followed by a sustained, deep US equity market drawdown. When considering the magnitude of market pullback, a return to the long-term average P/E alone implies 30% downside. In this scenario, our economics team models a resulting US recession, as described on page 4. SMH looks vulnerable: We think the first effects of an AI sell-off would be most striking in the SMH global semiconductor ETF. Composition is tilted to the US (82%), but it also has exposure to major AI players in Asia (11%) and Europe (7%). Leverage and retail participation are present in the ETF, which both have the potential to exacerbate any initial move lower. Any investors using SMH to position for the risks set out here would be likely to consider a put-ratio spread, but would then need to carefully manage rolling and restriking the trade around spot moves. Looking ahead, we maintain our projections for swift disinflation over the coming months. As some of the big price rises drop out of the annual rate calculation, slower administrative price rises by and large will see inflation (particularly services) drop lower through Q2-26, settling just around target. Slower wage growth will also help temper price rises, with margins constrained by more modest underlying demand. And government policy, combined with lower wholesale costs, will see dual fuel bills cut through the spring adding to the UK's disinflation. records.text: 1312/02/2026 Fed: Loss of independence FED: LOSS OF INDEPENDENCE Why it’s important: If the Federal Reserve acquiesces to a gradual erosion of its monetary policy independence, it could change its policy strategy to accommodate lower rates and permanently higher inflation. How it might happen: Personnel turnover, relentless criticism from the White House, and limited support from Congress take their toll. Norms shift gradually towards less and less appetite at the Fed for political conflict over monetary policy. Eventually, weak polling ahead of the mid-term elections leads the White House to demand big rate cuts and a fundamental change in policy strategy, and an exhausted Fed obliges. Which asset class is most exposed: As the public becomes convinced that the Fed is no longer pursuing 2% inflation as a policy goal, inflation expectations rise, the dollar weakens and the yield curve steepens. Freedom: Congress granted the Federal Reserve “operational independence” over monetary policy, allowing it to set interest rates to achieve broadly described goals over time. This independence (seen to varying extents throughout the world) allows the central bank to take actions that may be politically unpopular over the short run (like hiking rates) to achieve long-run goals (like low and stable inflation). Taiwan’s 2025 growth is heavily skewed to AI exports Taiwan’s 2025 full-year GDP grew at 8.7%, 75% of which was driven by increased net exports fueled by insatiable demand for Taiwan’s semiconductors and AI‑related products. The increase in Taiwan’s exports was entirely driven by tech products in the AI‑related space, and non‑tech products have not seen any positive growth since before 2023, while Taiwan’s AI‑export boom is expected to continue into 2026 and beyond. Despite the impressive headline GDP growth, the distributional gains from the AI‑export boom remain narrow and concentrated. Since 2023, virtually all gains in the TWSE have been in the electronics sector, and likely, the vast majority of the increase in industrial production and wage gains has also been concentrated in the small number of firms within the AI supply chain. By our estimation, around 5.4% of Taiwan’s labor force is directly engaged in the manufacturing of AI‑related products. records.text: n cost Finished lot cost The president has already postponed planned tariff hikes on lumber and furnishings, but existing tariffs on these and other key materials remain in place. The NAHB estimates that the cumulative effect of tariff actions has added nearly $11,000 to the cost of a typical new home. Applying a realized tariff rate of 22% on construction materials (based on the US ITC’s esti- mate of calculated duties) to the 7.3% import share of the average construction cost of $428,215 yields a lower estimate of about $7,000. However, it is important to note that the US ITC’s calculated duties do not account for additional anti- dumping or countervailing duties. Canadian softwood lum- ber—which constitutes nearly a quarter of total US supply— is currently subject to an extra 35% in such duties. Even if tariffs on building materials were scaled back com- prehensively—a scenario we see as unlikely—the complexity of global supply chains and the administration’s broader com- mitment to tariffs as a policy tool mean it would be difficult to fully insulate builders from higher input costs. records.text: To understand the potential size of a rise in Gilt yields should policy uncertainty rise further, we analyse previous examples of a rise in country risk in Gilt yields. We identify six episodes in recent years where the rise in country risk premium exceeded 15bp (note, we do not include the Gilt crisis of 2022, given the limited comparability to the current period following rate cuts and lower inflation). Exhibit 4 shows the rise in 10y Gilt yields over these periods, with the peak at around a 30bp increase in yields, which subsequently fades. Of course, a reasonable objection here is that a change of government / leadership would potentially result in a bigger source of uncertainty and thus a bigger rise in risk premium. While this is possible, we would say that at least some of these events shifted fiscal expectations, for example the reports suggesting no rise in the basic rate of income tax in the lead-up to the November 2025 budget. A way to calibrate how big a change in fiscal expectations is needed to generate a large move in Gilts, we rely on our previous work in mapping changes in medium-term deficit expectations to Gilt yields. We find that a 1pp increase in the medium-term budget deficit is worth around 35bp higher Gilt yields. records.text: the performance of EM FX shows a 3% depreciation against the USD in both nominal and real terms. What does this mean? In effect, US inflation performance has converged to the trade- weighted performance of its EM partners, meaning relative performance is being dictated by nominal movements in exchange rates, driven portfolio flows and relative equity performance and nominal yield spreads. Naturally there are exceptions to this rule and the most important of which is CNY. Exhibit 8 shows China’s trade-weighted exchange rate in both real and nominal terms over the same 4 year-period. Here we see that China’s inflation performance has diverged with its trading partners due to disinflation. The net result is that the CNY has depreciated by 15% in real terms, while the nominal trade-weighted value has lost 2.5%. The upshot is that recent CNY nominal appreciation against USD should have limited impact on competitiveness. Indeed, China’s stellar trade and export performance suggests China can afford CNY appreciation to alleviate trade tensions beyond the US and help to offset the concerns over trade diversion into Europe and ASEAN. To this end, while CNY appreciation against the USD is common consensus, CNY trade-weighted appreciation against its EM peers is being under-estimated by markets. records.text: Political risk is shifting and underpinning rising term premium Gilt 10y rates are underpinned by rising term premium How should the gilt market think about an environment of heightened and shifting political risk? Typically, it associates greater political risk with a steeper curve. Gilt 2/10s did steepen sharply, to about +90bp, but this has subsequently stalled. The curve dynamic can be best understood via the lens of term premium and what shifts in market pricing imply for the myriad of potential political outcomes. We can think of three basic cases: the first is where nothing really changes and the status quo prevails — in market space, that would mean the forward term structure is largely realised . A second, more adverse outcome would be something along the lines of a change of leadership that bolsters the Chancellor's position, since new leadership that might speak more openly about the need for more expansionist fiscal policy might wish to keep in post a Chancellor that the market associates with the existing fiscal architecture. A third (most adverse) outcome is Starmer and Reeves leaving their posts and the overall political/ fiscal architecture remaining undefined. The second and third scenarios would likely drive curve steepening but would see the term structure charge a higher premium for owning that outcome via more punishing carry. In ionic‑clay systems, rare earths occur adsorbed onto clay particles, rather than chemically locked in primary minerals. For Brazilian projects, this translates into: 1) lower mining costs, 2) reduced plant complexity, 3) lower energy requirements, and 4) lower investments compared to other regions. (Exhibit 5) Why hasn’t Brazil become a rare earth powerhouse yet? Brazil’s rare earth sector faces structural barriers that slow its ability to scale. The most immediate constraint is financing: unlike other major mining jurisdictions, Brazilian firms cannot use mining rights or future production as collateral, limiting domestic credit options and pushing developers toward foreign funding. records.text: 13 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 48 Deutsche Bank AG The elephant in the bond market room From a valuation perspective, the JGB2s30s flattener is the elephant in the bond market room, with a potential 100bp flattening. Real policy rates are too low on an absolute and cross-market basis given the wage dynamics. Long-dated forwards are too high on a cross-market basis given Japan’s external position. Now that the Japan election is behind us, the question is whether the policy choices of the incoming administration will support the flattening of the curve. Two weeks ago, we argued that the risk-reward was in favour of elephant hunting for two reasons. Firstly, high inflation is unlikely to be politically popular in a nation with significant private sector savings. This is increasingly reflected in opinion polls that have listed cost-of-living as the number one issue for voters by a significant margin. Abenomics 2.0 is therefore unlikely to be politically (let alone economically) sound in such an environment. Secondly, even though the BoJ did not provide a convincing hawkish signal at its last meeting, policymakers have subsequently demonstrated low tolerance for further weakness in currency and bond markets. Technical factors exacerbate rising yields: In the current Treasury market structure, primary dealers have limited balance sheet capacity and markets are overly reliant on high-frequency trading firms, which could make a Treasury sell- off disorderly. Additionally, as the sell-off after Liberation Day exposed investor positioning, long swap spread/futures basis positions and a perception of overseas investors fleeing Treasuries could drive a self-fulfilling rise in yields (see US rates: A self-propagating rise in yields? 9 April 2025). Against a backdrop of high inflation risks, plus the theoretical but unreliable backstop of the Standing Repo Program, the Fed, led by Kevin Warsh, takes its time to provide support to the Treasury market, which allows yields to rise unabated. A sovereign ratings downgrade adds fuel to the fire. Vicious feedback loop: Treasuries start to trade with a vicious feedback loop of higher yields→ higher interest costs→ wider deficits→ even-higher yields. A UST sell-off might be broad based as all investor bases question the risk-free status of USTs (unlike the Truss moment, which centered on the LDI investor base). But he also highlighted some pockets of concern. We remain comfortable with our view that the Fed won’t cut again under Powell. The European Council held another informal meeting this week to “brainstorm” these issues and pick up on the more than one year-old Draghi and Letta reports. This meeting is to prepare the next formal Council meeting in March. On trade, where the challenge from the US and China has recently helped push other deals over the line, openness and competition are still seen as the best way forward. Greater “pragmatism” has entered the discussion on managing some trade relationships. However, a diversified set of trade deals with different countries and country blocks is still seen as a good way of achieving objectives such as secure supplies of critical inputs. On the domestic side, efforts to cut red tape continue, with proposals and clear timelines being developed by the Com- mission for the next summit in March. Momentum is building on this, including via a proposed “28th regime” for company incorporations, sunset clauses in EU laws and a shift from directives to regulations to reduce the scope for national gold- plating of EU rules. The efficacy of such individual initiatives is hard to assess, but the sense of urgency is real. Merger guidelines are also being reviewed, with more support for “European champions” and “Buy European” initiatives in selected industries, at least if this would help boost invest- ment and innovation. Tail risk: Departure from fiscal prudence In this scenario, an individual who is considered to be far to the left of the Starmer government is chosen as prime minister, with a likely significant overhaul of fiscal policy, focused not only on the composition but likely also on aggregate policy, leading to an increase in borrowing. UK fiscal policy may no longer be on a tightening trajectory. Additional spending likely focuses on income support measures, day- to-day departmental spending, and nationalisation policies. Some of the increase in spending could be funded by higher taxes, possibly through a wealth tax. There is an increased risk that the fiscal rules and/or OBR oversight are scrapped. Fiscal risk premium spikes. 10y gilt yields could reach around 5.15%, with 5y5y around 5.95%. records.text: 13 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 44 Deutsche Bank AG Back to ample Money market conditions have improved markedly since the Fed started reserve management purchases in December. The triparty repo rate (TGCR) has moved from trading persistently above interest on reserve balances (IORB) at the end of last year to slightly below it. The effective fed funds rate (EFFR), the more stable of the two, has anchored itself at 1 bps below IORB after climbing rapidly from 7 bps below. The broad trend in these two money market rates could be particularly helpful for identifying major shifts in reserve conditions, as shown in today’s chart. This is a good indication that the Fed’s reserve management purchases (RMPs) are working to stabilize money market conditions. Other factors may have also contributed, such as seasonal bill paydowns from December through mid-January and dealer balance sheet redeployment after the year-end. Less attractive Treasury basis opportunities may also have reduced the demand for repo. However, these dynamics are fluid. Bill supply is on the rise again, and dealers could tighten balance sheets if they run into leverage constraints. Looking ahead, reserve management purchases are likely to continue at their current pace into the spring. Yet, GBP spreads have held up well, pointing to still-healthy demand and potentially elevated cash balances among investors (Exhibit 3 and Exhibit 4). More structurally, we think GBP spread resilience reflects a secular tightening in n sterling supply technicals: the share of foreign-domiciled issuers has declined from roughly 52% in 2015 to about 46% today, a trend that has coincided with non-UK issuers outperforming UK issuers. We think the decline in foreign participation has partly been for economic reasons given higher all-in yields in GBP vs. the EUR and USD market (Exhibit 5). Looking ahead, that tailwind may be fading. If the Bank of England cuts policy n rates as our economists expect, making GBP funding less punitive, non-UK supply could return at the margin. While lower rates and improved growth would be supportive for GBP credit fundamentals, we think the incremental supply impulse would be a net negative for spreads given already-stretched valuations. Hence, we think most of sterling’s spread outperformance is behind us and, within GBP , we prefer UK issuers vs. non-UK issuers. records.text: nths, where January prices could be compared against potentially downward biased November readings. However, the data do not indicate a material bias in those locations. The BLS also updated CPI seasonal factors with this release. As anticipated, the new factors partially corrected the strong seasonal push seen in 2025 (reducing it from 0.45% to 0.43%) and likely muted the acceleration in this month’s core CPI print. Overall, the revisions were minor. That said, seasonal factors merely redistribute inflation within the year. As a result, any January softness induced by the new factors should be offset by firmer prints later in the year. A simple comparison of pre and post revision core CPI series suggests that February is more likely to show more strength under the new factors. Turning to the details, core goods CPI came in softer than expected overall, but with notable dispersion. Used car prices were much weaker than our forecast, while other core goods (including appliances and electronics) were stronger. Our comparison of goods less versus more exposed to tariffs suggests that tariff pass through continued in January. OER was slightly softer than expected, which we view as payback for December’s strong print. We continue to estimate the underlying pace of rent inflation at roughly 0.27% m/ m. Finally, core services excluding housing accelerated—as is typical in January—potentially adding further support to the seasonal bias narrative.

In Scenario 2, we see risks of a moderate rise in inflation, moderate increase in bond supply, and therefore see higher yields than our current projections. In addition, we would expect the market to retain a certain amount of risk premium as the period of uncertainty would persist into the autumn budget, with a lack of clarity on which policies will ultimately be delivered, potential BoE response and ultimate tweaks to bond supply. If it is demonstrated that the new Cabinet is sticking to the fiscal rules, OBR oversight is maintained and new spending will be funded, we would expect risk premium to retrace, therefore with less impact on yields and ultimately the pound. Our projections for this scenario therefore embed one fewer BoE cut, 15bp upside to inflation and GBP15bn more in bond supply. These would put the 5y5y at 5.27– 5.37% based on our term premium framework, and the 10y at 4.70%, 25bp higher than current levels. However, the election of a new prime minister would merely begin an extended period of uncertainty, as the next fiscal event would likely not be until the autumn. We would therefore expect an inflated 5y5y, in a market navigating between Scenarios 2 and 3, more or less dependent on the new PM, until policy is unveiled. records.text: EGBs: soggy OATs crisp up Earlier this week, we published soggy OATs crisp up, in which we analysed the outlook for French spreads following year-to-date spread tightening. Given the recent passage of the 2026 Budget and failure of subsequent no-confidence motions, bearish impulses for OATs stemming from domestic politics appear likely to dry up for a few months to come. Municipal elections scheduled for March are one key event on the political calendar, but seem unlikely to spill over into political turbulence at the national level, in our view (although particular attention will be paid to RN's performance). While Le Pen's ongoing court appeal will also be worth following, it appears unlikely to reignite political risk premium for OATs in and of itself. The 2027 budget- setting process could pose more sizeable risks, but appears unlikely to gain investor attention until the summer at the earliest. And further ahead, the key political risk event for OATs will be the April 2027 presidential election, which will bring a range of tail scenarios for investors to fret over. Ultimately, we think ' when, not if' is still the state of play in terms of future bearish impulses for OATs stemming from domestic politics. But given the calendar ahead, we believe that moment is likely still many months away. With politics quietening down, we think OATs should continue to enjoy a TINA (there is no alternative) dynamic. records.text: Consumption tax cuts to boost real GDP during implementation period Nominal GDP likely to decline, contrary to real GDP Three scenarios based on funding sources We begin by considering the economic impact of consumption tax cuts. The effects on real GDP can be divided into two channels. The first is the reduction in households’ financial burden through lower tax‑inclusive prices, which stimulates consumption. This effect is likely to be particularly strong for households that allocate most of their income to consumption and have limited savings, as the additional disposable income generated by tax cuts is more likely to be spent rather than saved. The second channel is the intertemporal shifting of consumption from outside the tax‑cut period into the period itself. In particular, in the period immediately preceding the tax cut, households are likely to defer purchases, especially of processed goods that are ordinarily stockpiled, leading to weaker consumption. Conversely, consumption is likely to rise sharply immediately after the tax cut is implemented due to a rebound effect ( Figure 7). Similarly, just before the tax cut expires, frontloaded demand is likely to emerge, followed by a subsequent decline in consumption once the tax cut ends. Taken together, these effects suggest that real GDP is boosted during the tax‑cut period, but negative effects are likely to materialize both before and after the period, particularly immediately ahead of and following its implementation.

The relative strength of PCE versus CPI appears to be driven by a sharp increase in legal services inflation (roughly +11% m/m). For the Fed, the sudden increase in prices in January might not be new information. The Fed is aware of the typical strength in core inflation in January. Today’s report provided mixed evidence on the seasonal acceleration typically observed at the start of the year. While some goods and services categories behaved as expected— such as recreation services, car parts, and recreation commodities—other categories that are usually upward biased did not show the strength we anticipated. Seasonality appears to have been more pronounced in PCE, largely due to a significant reset in legal services prices, which our calculations suggest rose about 11% SA. However, it is the relative backdrop that is key for Dollar performance and its n relationship with US equities. While the “Deepseek” episode represented a potential shift in the global beneficiaries of AI from the US to the rest of the world and, in turn, had clear negative implications for future relative asset performance, growth prospects, and ultimately for the Dollar, the more recent software selloff is less clearly a US-specific negative shock. Most recently, US-specific negative shocks that trigger “Dollar down, equities n down” episodes have been driven by US policy uncertainty. In this context, the Dollar’s consolidation last week was also consistent with more conciliatory US macro policy. Core CPI came in below forecasts eight times and above only once— last January. That made 2025 the softest year for core‑inflation relative to expectations in over a decade (Figure 1). But will that pattern extend into 2026 or have forecasters learnt their lesson? For our part, State Street PriceStats projections performed better than many, anticipating seven of the eight downside surprises last year (Figure 2), although we had also anticipated a softer reading in July that didn’t materialise. We also missed last January’s upside surprise. For January 2026, our signals are more mixed. The aggregate series was close to seasonal norms (Figure 3), implying a central headline CPI estimate of 0.15% sa m/m, helped by softer vehicle‑fuel prices that pulled down transportation. But firmer‑than‑usual rebounds in recreation/electronics and apparel push our core CPI estimate to 0.32% sa m/m—the highest in four months. Even so, that estimate aligns with consensus and remains lower than last January; the trend in lower annual core inflation rates will continue. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 313/02/2026 Fiscal concerns at centre stage: Since the 2022 UK mini-budget under Prime Minister Liz Truss, UK markets have exhibited a heightened sensitivity to fiscal policy developments or any sign of a move away from fiscal prudence. The market showed this sensitivity at various points in 2025, for instance following rumours that Chancellor Rachel Reeves would be removed, and over recent weeks. There are a lot of unknowns still at play, particularly on the leading candidates’ fiscal policy priorities. While the market may fear a ‘mini-budget 2.0’ moment following any leftward shift, we think it is more likely that there would be a shift in the composition of policy toward more spending and more taxes. Ultimately, a number of dynamics would be considered, including the aggregate fiscal policy stance, compositional shifts in policy, temporal shifts in policy, and whether the guardrails around fiscal policy are maintained (e.g. the fiscal rules and the Office for Budget Responsibility. Each of these presents a potential challenge to the credibility of fiscal plans and will be a consideration for market participants. Figure 5 outlines three possible scenarios. Though we do not define a base case given the high degree of uncertainty, we consider the first two scenarios to be more likely outcomes than the tail-risk scenario and do not see material differences between their macroeconomic implications as the aggregate fiscal stance

As enterprises increasingly adopt multi-model strategies— often deploying 2-3 general-purpose LLMs—the bulk of value from rising AI spend, deeper platform integration, and data capture will eventually accrue to the primary model provider that can deliver cutting-edge agentic capabilities and tools that drive tangible ROI. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 213/02/2026 Slow fiscal consolidation: In terms of Israel’s fiscal outlook for 2026, consensus expects a consolidation, albeit a relatively slow one (Figure 2). The government has approved a deficit target of 3.9% of GDP for this year. The budget bill is currently making its way through the committee stage, with final approval expected by the end of March. We estimate the cash deficit will average about ILS85bn in 2026 and 2027, tighter than the ILS98bn in 2025. Strong nominal GDP growth, with consensus forecasts at around 6.5% for 2026, alongside cross-border tech M&A deals, should support tax receipts this year. Defence spending was elevated in 2025 at ILS165bn, compared to the ILS125bn recommendation that the Nagel committee made in early 2025. The approved number for 2026 is ILS138bn, and, significantly, in our view, the defence budget has not been linked to GDP, which should keep a lid on spending in the medium-term. Financing mix diversified: The financing mix of Israel’s issuance has been relatively stable for the past two years (Figure 3). Some 50% of domestic issuance is via ILGOVs, slightly less than 30% in linkers and the rest is a mixture of bills, floaters and non-tradable bonds. Compared to the rest of EM, Israel has one of the lowest shares of total debt into fixed coupon bonds at 52%, relative to an average of about 74% for EM and CEEMEA, according to BIS data. Fiscal policy: More generally our view is that fiscal policy is unlikely to change dramatically over the next year under any scenario. In the case of a Tisza victory we think it would take time for any new government to quickly unwind the existing, loose fiscal policy measures. records.text: nths, where January prices could be compared against potentially downward biased November readings. However, the data do not indicate a material bias in those locations. The BLS also updated CPI seasonal factors with this release. As anticipated, the new factors partially corrected the strong seasonal push seen in 2025 (reducing it from 0.45% to 0.43%) and likely muted the acceleration in this month’s core CPI print. Overall, the revisions were minor. That said, seasonal factors merely redistribute inflation within the year. As a result, any January softness induced by the new factors should be offset by firmer prints later in the year. A simple comparison of pre and post revision core CPI series suggests that February is more likely to show more strength under the new factors. Turning to the details, core goods CPI came in softer than expected overall, but with notable dispersion. Used car prices were much weaker than our forecast, while other core goods (including appliances and electronics) were stronger. Our comparison of goods less versus more exposed to tariffs suggests that tariff pass through continued in January. OER was slightly softer than expected, which we view as payback for December’s strong print. We continue to estimate the underlying pace of rent inflation at roughly 0.27% m/ m. Finally, core services excluding housing accelerated—as is typical in January—potentially adding further support to the seasonal bias narrative.

records.text: The methodology: Finding multiple ways to win as corporate governance momentum improves In this report, we screen a universe of 430 listed Japanese companies trading with a 6M adtv of over US$10mn to identify names that are exposed to eight corporate governance-related factors. We believe that exposure to one or more of these factors could significantly increase the probability of near-term corporate governance-related announcements by management. The eight factors are: 1) Share buyback momentum; 2) An activist investor currently on the shareholder register; 3) Large cross-shareholdings-to-net-assets ratio; 4) Large number of operating segments; 5) Net cash and ROE below 8%; 6) Unrealized real estate gains of at least 5% of market capitalization; 7) In the bottom 10% of 2025 AGM management approval rates; 8) CY2025 share price under-performance. We have then included companies that appear in at least 3 of these screens in a final screen-of-screens shown in Exhibit 1 below. We believe this cohort of 18 listed Japanese companies above may have a higher probability of enhancing corporate governance measures during CY2026 1H. Such moves could increase the possibility of these companies, either individually or collectively, outperforming the broader index from here. Within the eight factors highlighted above, we note that a low AGM approval rating appears to be one of the better predictors of strong out-performance. records.text: Marija Veitmane 12 February 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General European stocks are running on fumes European stocks performed strongly in 2025, gaining nearly 20% (in EUR), despite virtually no earnings growth. Investors believed that earnings would grow this year and had re-priced stocks higher. We are increasingly seeing signs of those hopes being dashed – analysts are downgrading earnings growth expectations while institutional investors are selling European stocks. The market’s reaction to 4Q earnings highlights the unreasonable optimism for the region. So far 144 European companies reported their earnings, and the results were good but not great. The proportion of companies exceeding analysts’ expectations is just over 60%, slightly less than global average (66%) and far below US (80%), while average earnings surprise is also smaller than global and US averages. Perhaps the relative rarity of earnings beats explains why prices jump so much when results exceed those expectations. It is puzzling as to why the market is rewarding earnings misses in Europe, but nowhere else (Figure 1). One possible explanation could be strong management guidance. However, this is hardly plausible as Europe is the region with the largest EPS downgrades globally. Unlike in Germany or Italy, we focus not (mainly) about growth, nor (mainly) about the public finance trajectory. And it is not about the 2027 presidential election either (not yet, at least). It’s about disinflation, and how rapid this process has been in France – in fact perhaps, too rapid. In France, disinflation is “holistic”: consumer price inflation is well below 2% in both core and headline. Even services HICP is already back at 2% yoy (see Exhibit 1). We expect 1.3% inflation this year and 1.5% next. We cut 2027 by 20bp as we take out ETS2 (Emission Trading System) effects from the profile. Our forecasts are well below the Euro area average at 1.7% each year. It’s not just consumer prices. Wage growth has slowed to c 1.5% across various indicators. Labour productivity growth has resumed from lower levels but at a faster pace than pre-Covid. The labour market has plateaued; prominent shortages during the post-Covid rebound have disappeared. Lastly, unit profits have come well off their highs, too, further and faster than the Euro area aggregate. That’s quite a unique combination of data, akin to properly holistic inflation. On the legislative front, after an overnight session on Wednesday the Senate approved the Labor Reform, with 42 votes in favor and 30 against. As we highlighted in our recent note, the project makes working conditions more flexible and offers incentives for the formalization of workers and job cre- ation. It also modifies Labor Justice to discourage the so- called trial industry. There were late concessions to secure votes, including changes across multiple articles. Indeed, the fiscal chapter around corporate income-tax rate cuts was pulled back to avoid conflict with governors, while other tax- related delegations to the Economy Ministry were curtailed in the final text. The bill now moves to the Chamber of Depu- ties, where the government is working to reach agreements and avoid further modifications, with hopes that the debate will reach the Lower House by the end of next week. records.text: ab 13 February 2026 Global Research US Economic Perspectives January CPI recap: Not a bad as expected January CPI buffeted by many factors, take little signal Today's CPI release (0.17% headline CPI increase, 0.30% core CPI increase) surprised somewhat to the downside of consensus, but we suggest taking little signal from the surprise in today's CPI report. Today's report had a number of special factors that mean it may not be a good guide to the underlying pace of inflation.  The January CPI incorporates revisions to seasonal adjustment factors and item relative importance weights. These factors make the January CPI more difficult to predict. In today's release the seasonal adjustment factors for January were revised down. Using last year's seasonal adjustment factors we estimate that the core CPI would have risen 0.33% rather than the 0.30% published in today's report. The greater push down in the revised seasonal factors is a reflection that January CPIs have tended to be on the strong side in recent years. Nonetheless, we think today's revision probably does not go far enough and the monthly growth rate for the core CPI this year will likely average less than the 0.30% in today's report.  Reversal of the impact of the late start of November sampling : Sampling for the November CPI did not begin until November 14th after the government shutdown ended. This pushed the collection of price quotes into late November and the holidays might have affected those November prices.

Our in-house data-surprise trackers for Hungary reveal an economy which has generally underperformed expectations compared with the country’s last election cycle in 2022 (Figure 2). Growth remains below trend, undershooting that of regional peers, with economic weakness driven primarily by a deep manufacturing recession and poor investment levels. This reflects both a struggling industrial sector and very limited access to EU funds. Inflation meanwhile has proved more stubborn in recent years, with notable stickiness in services. Wage pressures, though moderating gradually, are still elevated and have not been fully matched by output gains (productivity) – see CEEMEA: Labour market key to squeeze out services CPI, dated 14 October 2025. Consumer sentiment rally fails to shift perceptions: Hungary has finally started to see a bounce in consumer sentiment recently, likely indicating that inflation has started to fall. The two obvious factors to show that are the unemployment rate and wage growth; yes, the Philipps curve candidates are back. The French unemployment rate rises from 7.1% at its trough in 2022 (abstracting from the 6.9% from peak Covid lockdown and short time work periods), to 7.7% by end-27E. This reflects continued labour force growth rather than job losses and also helped to ease apparent labour force shortages and hiring difficulties prominent surveys during the post-Covid rebound. Wage growth has responded very quickly to both higher energy-price induced inflation and then disinflation, and arguably also labour market normalisation from tight levels. France reported negotiated wage growth at 1.6% yoy, private sector wage growth at 1.4% yoy and compensation per employee growth at 1.4% in 3Q25, with no apparent wage drift Exhibit 9. Of course, wage growth without a glimpse at productivity growth would be misleading. The focus on the drop in French labour productivity measures after Covid has vanished and perhaps for obvious reasons: the gap to Euro area productivity levels, at least vs 2019 reference points, has closed. records.text: B does not appear to have meaningfully increased its FX reserves for at least a year, suggesting they have largely been absent from the FX market, allowing CHF to appreciate. That said, we would note that the REER is now currently at levels where, based on our estimates, the SNB has previously intervened to sell CHF (A closer look at SNB FX intervention, 7 Feb 2024) (Figure 25). Though not to a large enough extent to reverse the trend in the nominal exchange rate, these interventions have been enough to slow nominal appreciation such that the REER can depreciate (Figure 26). The incentive to intervene in FX comes from the continued drag from foreign components on YoY CPI, which is a function of the strong currency (Figure 27). Our simple base effects model implies a good chance that Swiss CPI remains negative through to October, and given the often-cited high bar to negative interest rates (SwissInfo, 21 Jan), intermittent FX interventions could well be an effective way of managing deflation risks. Given that, our base case is for EURCHF to continue to depreciate, but at a slow rate as the SNB gently leans against it. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: Dissents by the central bank head are quite rare, having only occurred three times at the Fed (in the 1930s), twice at the BoE, and once at the Riksbank (left chart, Exhibit 3). Furthermore, the preferred policy path of dissenting leaders is often adopted in future meetings, as was the case for Czech National Bank (CNB) Governor Singer in 2012 and BoE Governor King in 2007 (right chart, Exhibit 3). In Exhibit 4, we regress the policy decision at a given meeting on the dissent spread at the preceding meetings—defined as the share of the committee dissenting in favor of a more hawkish move minus the share dissenting in favor of a more dovish move—to test whether dissents predict future policy moves. The dissent measure considered in these regressions is equal to zero when there are no dissents or an equal number of hawkish and dovish dissents. Consensus estimates for 2026 AI hyperscaler capex have increased to $659 billion, reflecting 60% growth vs. 2025, up from $539 billion at the start of earnings season. records.text: Why it’s important: Private credit debt growth has surged and so have investor allocations to this asset class. With no historical precedent, we map out potential catalysts of fundamental stress that could drive default losses and a liquidity crunch in leveraged finance markets. How it might happen: Disruption in the tech sector challenges legacy software businesses, among the largest industries in private credit. This drives a drop in the net asset values of business development companies, which challenges asset coverage tests or even forces asset sales to meet liquidity needs. Which asset class is most exposed: Credit markets with lending to middle- market borrowers are most vulnerable to a liquidity crunch, including BDCs, leveraged loans, and CLOs. Investors would demand a higher fundamental risk premium for smaller tech borrowers. BDCs would underperform with dispersion across managers. Private credit CLOs would price in the prospect of higher risks of downgrade to below investment grade, triggering selling pressure. 10 Sources: Preqin (left-hand chart), Bloomberg (right-hand chart), BNP Paribas PRIVATE CREDIT: FUNDAMENTAL DETERIORATION DRIVES LIQUIDITY CRUNCH 12/02/2026 Private credit: Fundamental deterioration drives liquidity crunch David Nochimowski, Global Head of CLO & ABS Strategy | BNP Paribas Representative Office – Israel | Meghan Robson, Head of US Credit Strategy and US Desk Analysts | BNP Paribas Securities Corp. We have seen early signs of a broadening out in manufacturing activity. • Broader investment should contribute to better labor demand this year and improve the foundation of the economic expansion. AI investment isn’t going anywhere yet AI related investment was a big story in 2025. It contributed to the acceleration seen in investment in computers and peripheral equipment, software, data centers, and research and development. Together these categories contributed an average of 0.9pp to GDP growth through the first three quarters of 2025 (Exhibit 1). Meanwhile, all other nonresidential investment had little effect on growth over the same period. To be sure not all of investment in these categories can be chalked up to AI. Also, much of the equipment category is imported. Therefore, the role AI investment played in growth is much smaller than what the investment numbers suggest. Still, AI was a big factor in last year’s surprisingly resilient investment data as fiscal stimulus for green energy and semiconductors faded.
