records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 13 February 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS Is AI disinflationary? Not so fast… The recently nominated Fed Chair started a debate on whether the disinflationary forces created by the AI revolution justify further rate cuts by the Fed. The argument goes that AI-driven technologies will boost productivity growth, reduce costs and create a virtuous dynamic of higher growth and lower inflation that needs to be accommodated with lower interest rates. We think there is not yet enough evidence that this will be the case, and in the best case scenario, these improvements in productivity materialize in the long run, the short run dynamics of inflation will be dictated by the associated boom in investment and consumption that precedes the productivity boom. In addition, higher productivity growth means higher, not lower, real neutral rates. The long run: lower cost of production Can the AI revolution reduce the production costs of the economy and therefore higher non-inflationary long run growth? Yes, assuming those improvements in technology really take place, which is uncertain at this point, at least its scope. Productivity growth means the economy can use its resources more efficiently and produce the same with less resources or more with the same resources. While labor market news has kept very near-term Fed n pricing anchored and longer-term yields within the context of the last several months’ trading range, the mix of AI wobbles and recently bullish global spillovers have dominated recent price action. Those factors have corresponded to a downshift in terminal rate pricing alongside a relatively stable curve shape further out—visible in the sharper flattening in 2s5s versus more limited shifts in 5s10s and 10s30s curves. Uncertainty around when any potential disruption might show up more clearly in the macroeconomic data can see this dynamic continue in the near-term—pricing more cuts over time, rather than faster or sooner—but a sufficiently large extension in the risk off tone should eventually reintroduce steepening pressure as growth worries come to the fore. And while real rates have done much of the heavy lifting in driving the move lower in forward yields (Exhibit 1), we would expect any meaningful extension of the current risk off tone to extend to the inflation forwards. records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 28 November) Real GDP contracted in Q3 for the first negative growth in six quarters, reflecting a sharp drop in housing investment and sluggish exports linked to tariffs. However, as the former was driven by institutional factors, we expect a return to positive growth from Q4. Looking ahead, we expect growth of around 1% on average due primarily to firm capital investment on the back of structural factors such as labor-saving expenditures and stable consumption stemming from a recovery in the real income environment under slowing inflation. Although the economic measures decided by the Takaichi administration are limited in terms of their growth-boosting effect relative to scale, they are likely to provide a certain degree of support to the economy. On the price front, we expect CPI inflation excluding perishables (core) to ease as a trend, albeit with fluctuations, in the near term due mainly to declines (y/y base effects) in goods, especially food. However, inflation is increasingly sticky, suggesting any deceleration will be more moderate than we previously expected. Furthermore, services inflation has become increasingly robust as the dynamic synergy between wages and prices strengthens on the back of irreversible structural changes in the labor market. We expect the latter to partially offset the former, with inflation remaining in the 2% handle into early 2027 before stabilizing around 1.8%. Monetary policy (last updated

The EU ETS rapidly appears to be becoming the political scapegoat for the lack of EU’s industrial competitiveness, despite its marginal burden, at less than 1% of aggregate industrial gross value (GVA) added through 2030. The dominant burden comes from gas and power, even inflated by taxes and levies generally exceeding 30% of the final price paid – even higher for non-large industrial entities (for instance Italy’s public broadcasting license fee is layered on the electricity bill, adding up to 12-15% extra costs on average). We doubt lower EUA prices will deliver any boost to EU industry’s competitiveness as implied in the rhetoric. Yet the narrative risks genuine, self-inflicted harm: Less fiscal revenues for member States, EU budget delaying compliance, weakening investment confidence, and adding volatility that hurts even major industrial names – for instance, large European cement stocks that were beneficiaries of the narrative of increasing EUA prices have taken a hit: Indeed, cement is a series of micro- markets given transportation economics, as cement cannot travel more than 300- 500km by land, while allowances are given by plant, not by company. Oth- er suggestions for mortgage rate relief include: • Reducing guarantee fees (G-fees) and insurance pre- miums (MIPs): Lowering the FHA’s fees for first-time buyers could allow the GSEs to reduce their own fees for other borrowers. However, any cut to FHA MIPs would likely result in an even more modest reduction in G-fees. • 50-year mortgage products: These longer-term loans would carry a higher rate—our MBS analysts estimate that rates might need to be about 50bp higher than on a standard 30-year mortgage—but would help reduce monthly payments. An unintended consequence could be stronger “lock-in,” as slower equity buildup would make it harder to later move up to a larger home. • Prepay penalty mortgages: This structure would offer a lower rate in exchange for a penalty if the borrower refi- nances or pays off the mortgage early. Our MBS analysts estimate that this product could lower rates about 45bp. • “Portable” mortgages: Allowing borrowers to transfer existing mortgages to new homes could help ease “lock- in”, but would likely require congressional approval. records.text: the RBA reversed course last week and delivered the first hike of the cycle. A surprise resurgence in domestic price pressures in 2H25 was the catalyst for the about-face, with both headline and trimmed mean inflation now tracking above the top of the RBA’s target band. This marks the shortest interval between policy pivots since 2009, raising questions about the true restrictiveness of policy settings and the drivers behind the previous disinflationary impulse from 2H22. Here we focus on the latter, comparing the current inflation backdrop to the 2021/2022 episode and the implications for monetary policy. Go your own way Apart from the obvious difference in magnitudes, perhaps the most salient difference from the 2021–22 inflation spike is that today’s price pressures look more home‑grown and idio- syncratic, with Australian and global headline inflation decoupling since mid‑2025 (Figure 1). In 2021–22, powerful synchronized global supply shocks—logistics bottlenecks, elevated freight costs, and commodity surges—and demand recoveries pushed prices sharply higher across most econo- mies. Broad‑based DM tightening and the unwinding of earli- er frictions delivered much of the disinflation through 2023. Now, those common global drivers have faded relative to domestic forces, with Australia’s inflation pulse more idio- syncratic. 0 2 4 6 8 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 Global Australia %oya Figure 1: Australian vs global inflation Source: ABS, J.P. records.text: Simulating consumption tax cuts assuming implementation in FY26 Another point to watch is appointments to the Policy Board. Board Member Noguchi (an advocate of reflationary policy) will complete his five‑year term at the end of March, while Board Member Nakagawa (a centrist) will reach the end of her term at the end of June. Policy Board appointments are determined through a process in which the government selects candidates and obtains approval from both houses of the Diet. According to Reuters, a successor candidate for Board Member Noguchi could be presented to the Diet as early as 25 February. Whom PM Takaichi – buoyed by her landslide victory in the general election – chooses to appoint could shed light on her future stance toward monetary policy. US-Japan summit to see a focus on any requests for increased defense spending Figure 4 lists key upcoming events. First, a special Diet session will be convened in 18 February, during which deliberations on the FY26 budget will take place. PM Takaichi’s next critical moment will come at the US-Japan summit meeting on 19 March. Because this meeting takes place just before President Trump’s planned visit to China in April, it carries extremely high significance for security policy. For Takaichi, it represents a major opportunity to demonstrate to the world the strong relationship of trust she has built with President Trump. It was surprising to us that the economy has manoeuvred the economic policy uncertainty shock from the 2024 snap elections quite so well (Exhibit 8). Partially, external price competitiveness may have helped to buffer the potential effects on the economy via domestic demand, although the EUR appreciation of 2025 and the EURUSD appreciation at the beginning of this year tone down the effect. But to a larger extent, fiscal policy may have come to the rescue, albeit accidentally. Don’t get us wrong: the 2023 fiscal slippage and its lasting deterioration on the forward looking deficit trajectory meaningfully weighs on our otherwise still benign structural view on France. Large institutional investors began to play a more prominent role in the single-family home market following the GFC. While investors account for around 17% of single- family home sales, up from a pre-GFC average of below 10% (Figure 6), the majority of these purchases are made by small- er investors. Large institutional investors only own around 3% of the single-family rental stock (Fallon et al., 2023; Ellen and Goodman, 2023). Our real estate analysts estimate that these investors own less than 1% of the overall housing stock. 14 18 22 26 30 34 38 8 12 16 20 24 28 32 05 10 15 20 25 %, 4-quarter moving average; both scales Figure 6: Investor share of home purchases Source: Redfin, J.P. records.text: nd revision we have made this year in the direction of our "animal spirits" upside scenario. Our previous forecast revision was primarily based on resiliency in consumer spending, while this revision carries forward strength in business spending. Revisions to employment data point to faster productivity While resiliency in consumer and business spending have tilted our forecast toward our demand-driven upside scenario, other data point in the direction of our supply-side driven upside scenario (see Exhibit 24 for a sketch of alternative scenarios to our baseline outlook). Annual benchmark revisions to employment reduced the level of nonfarm payrolls in March 2025 by 836k. When applied to monthly payrolls from April 2024 to March 2025, the revisions reduce average monthly payroll gains over this time period by 72k. In addition, monthly payroll gains from April to December 2025 were revised lower by an average of 11k per month. Downward revisions to payrolls imply faster productivity growth in prior years (assuming future GDP revisions are minor in nature). We estimate that the four-quarter change in nonfarm business productivity in terms of real output per worker rose 2.4% through 3Q 25, up from 1.9% previously.

records.text: 13 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 11 In sum, we are expecting a pick-up in m/m inflation for both core services and core goods from December. Alternative indicators point to a rebound in used car prices, while we project positive m/m inflation for new cars and another strong increase in apparel prices. In services, the pick-up mainly comes from the assumption that the December ‘outliers’ are not repeated, while we expect somewhat softer m/m prints for lodging away, airfares and rent/OER, where new rent indicators imply that inflation remains on a gradual softening trend. Energy prices are likely to have declined (-1% m/m), while our bottom-up indicators suggest that food inflation has slowed from its December pace. A weak trend in agricultural prices is likely to mean that food price momentum remains benign for now. Looking ahead, while headline year-on-year inflation is likely to fall in January, it is projected to rise again between February and May and mostly stay in a 2.5%-2.9% range through this year. We expect growth to pick up in both economies; labour markets look soft across the UK and the US; inflation is likely to cool materially on both sides of the Atlantic as special factors drop out; and we expect the BoE and Fed to normalise monetary policy this year. records.text: o recap, gilt supply days had a significant bearish impact in 4Q24 and into 1Q25, coinciding with a higher fiscal risk premium after the 30 October 2024 Budget - Figure 7. There was then relief in 2Q25 with the DMO’s sharp pivot shorter in the WAM of primary issuance. Fiscal uncertainty started to build again in 3Q25 with a long wait ahead of the 26 November Budget. Supply days then turned more supportive since 4Q25 as reports began to emerge in October of plans to increase headroom combined with healthy issuance progress by the DMO. The good news for gilts is that there is unlikely to be a need to revisit fiscal policy until the autumn Budget. Indeed, the 2026 Budget is already starting to feel like a future pivotal moment for gilts. Base case is that whoever is in charge will likely feel constrained by gilts and unable to materially increase borrowing. The EU ETS rapidly appears to be becoming the political scapegoat for the lack of EU’s industrial competitiveness, despite its marginal burden, at less than 1% of aggregate industrial gross value (GVA) added through 2030. The dominant burden comes from gas and power, even inflated by taxes and levies generally exceeding 30% of the final price paid – even higher for non-large industrial entities (for instance Italy’s public broadcasting license fee is layered on the electricity bill, adding up to 12-15% extra costs on average). We doubt lower EUA prices will deliver any boost to EU industry’s competitiveness as implied in the rhetoric. Yet the narrative risks genuine, self-inflicted harm: Less fiscal revenues for member States, EU budget delaying compliance, weakening investment confidence, and adding volatility that hurts even major industrial names – for instance, large European cement stocks that were beneficiaries of the narrative of increasing EUA prices have taken a hit: Indeed, cement is a series of micro- markets given transportation economics, as cement cannot travel more than 300- 500km by land, while allowances are given by plant, not by company. records.text: curve. From a markets standpoint, this argues for SOFR to trade above FF, with additional risk premium. Higher term premium: Absent full coordination, the market would likely anticipate longer- duration supply during the transition. Were the Treasury to replace lost SOMA add-ons by raising coupon issuance, we estimate that 10y-equivalent supply could be cumulatively higher by $1.7trn in five years' time versus the status quo. We believe that is worth 40-50bp in additional term premium in 10s. Even if the Treasury kept issuance the same for now, the market could conclude that its willingness to have more T-bills in outstanding debt is transitory and that it will eventually increase issuance across the curve. Higher cut premium in the front end: We believe he Fed will ultimately have to use the policy rate tool to offset the adverse effect of any tightening of financial conditions. Hence, any increase in term premium would, all else equal, warrant an offsetting decrease in the policy rate. Overall, we believe the yield curve should be steeper. 12 February 2026 8 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: It's complicated

records.text: US Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 4 Fixed Income Blogs What could Warsh mean for the Fed’s balance sheet? Matthew Raskin | Strategist | +1-212-250-1741 Matthew Luzzetti, Ph.D. | Chief US Economist | +1-212-250-6161 Steven Zeng, CFA | Strategist | +1-212-250-9373 Andrew Fu | Strategist | +1-212-250-1743 Note: This note was originally published on 10 February 2026. Introduction A prior note discussed the potential implications of Kevin Warsh’s nomination as Fed chair. It highlighted his critiques of Fed policy and claims that a smaller Fed balance sheet could reduce inflation and allow for lower policy rates. Here we consider various ways the Fed could plausibly achieve a smaller or less active balance sheet or securities portfolio, or one with less duration risk, as well as related considerations. In doing so, we separately discuss the current balance sheet, both size and composition, and potential future asset purchases. Overall, we see the most likely path to a smaller balance sheet as coming through regulatory changes that reduce bank reserves demand, though adjustments to the Fed’s ample reserve regime could also allow for a smaller securities portfolio. With respect to portfolio composition, the Fed is reducing its MBS holdings and could speed that process with sales. records.text: M Update 2 January CPI CPI came in below expectations, with core prices rising 0.30% m/m in January (MS: 0.36%, consensus: 0.3%) and headline prices up 0.17% m/m (MS: 0.37%). This leaves core CPI at 2.55% y/y and headline CPI at 2.38% y/y in January. Based on this print, we raised our January core PCE inflation forecast to 0.49% m/m, from 0.38% prior to the CPI release. The relative strength of PCE versus CPI appears to be driven by a sharp increase in legal services inflation (roughly +11% m/m). For the Fed, the sudden increase in prices in January might not be new information. The Fed is aware of the typical strength in core inflation in January. Today’s report provided mixed evidence on the seasonal acceleration typically observed at the start of the year. While some goods and services categories behaved as expected— such as recreation services, car parts, and recreation commodities—other categories that are usually upward biased did not show the strength we anticipated. Seasonality appears to have been more pronounced in PCE, largely due to a significant reset in legal services prices, which our calculations suggest rose about 11% SA. As expected, there was little evidence of shutdown-related noise. The main risk was higher measured inflation in cities surveyed only in odd months, where January prices could be compared against potentially downward biased November readings. records.text: 14 Global Economic Weekly | 13 February 2026 The labor-income transmission of the AI boom is narrow: technology-related manufacturing and services employ less than 14% of Taiwan's industrial and services employees, or about 5% of the population. Financial assets remain concentrated among high-net-worth households, limiting the aggregate consumption response to wealth gains. Upgrade inflation forecasts to 1.6%/2.0% in 2026/27 Reflecting this more constructive yet uneven consumption backdrop, we revise our inflation forecasts to 1.6% and 2.0% for 2026 and 2027, respectively, up from 1.3% and 1.7%. This trajectory points to a gradual recovery in total private-sector demand while imported inflation remains subdued. Our updated outlook also factors in currency stabilization, as the earlier TWD appreciation was a key deflationary force in 2025. Meanwhile, services inflation firmed in 4Q25, with stickier components-dining, housing, and education and entertainment-reflecting stronger domestic consumption demand and a gradual buildup in underlying inflationary pressure. records.text: With the upcoming Greater Manchester by-election on 26 February and local elections on 7 May, ongoing political uncertainty is likely to keep this risk premium elevated. Although Gilts have ultimately rallied over recent quarters, including following the November 2025 budget, the market will likely focus on the potential fiscal impact from any change in government leadership. Given the current plan for budget consolidation (albeit a gradual one), a shift towards taxation measures with higher revenue uncertainty, greater spending commitments, or looser fiscal rules would likely result in a deterioration of medium-term fiscal or inflation expectations. Below we attempt to benchmark the market pricing of risk premium against prior episodes of policy uncertainty. In addition to our term premium model, another way to visualise risk premium in Gilts is via our country risk premium framework. This model generates a breakdown of Gilt yields via a sign restriction technique to identify macro factors – the country risk premium is the factor derived from a simultaneous price decline in UK bonds, equities and Sterling. This measure shows a modest rise in risk premium despite the rally in Gilts in the last few sessions of around 10bp (Exhibit 3). records.text: ign central banks), which has a current balance of around $320bn. Reducing securities holdings For a given level of total assets, the Fed’s securities portfolio could be reduced. This would most likely entail using repo. One approach could be to use repo to help efficiently run an ample regime, particular amid uncertain shifts in reserve demand, in what some refer to as a “demand-driven floor system.” In this setup, the Fed’s securities portfolio would be sized to leave reserves in s tructural deficiency , and price-based repo operations would be used to fill the gap. This could shrink the balance sheet by eliminating any excess reserves buffer, but more importantly would substitute repo for Treasuries and MBS and thus lower the Fed’s duration footprint. Other major central banks , such as the BoE, effectively operate various forms of a demand-driven floor system. Another approach would be to use repo operations to sterilize the reserve impact of TGA fluctuations. Here the Fed would roughly match TGA balances with repo, the result of which would be a smaller securities portfolio over time. We first heard of the idea from Bill Nelson, chief economist at BPI; it was subsequently mentioned in Governor Miran’s first speech after joining the Fed. A separate possibility being discussed again is to revalue the Fed’s gold holdings. With its policy approaching the neutral range, the Monetary Policy Committee has already shown a preference for a cautious approach to further rate cuts. Elevated political volatility and uncertainty are likely to reinforce this, as the MPC weighs the prospect of expansionary fiscal policy against a potential tightening in financial conditions and the negative impact of depressed consumer and business sentiment. This backdrop of elevated political uncertainty has been a central component of our UK macroeconomic projections since Global Outlook 2026: In a good place (dated 1 December 2025) – were it not for the political uncertainty, our projections for the UK economy would have been more favourable. Once policy announcements are formalised through a budget process, this could prompt the BoE to reconsider the path for monetary policy. Further focus on fiscal tightening and disinflationary policy measures could make the case for additional rate cuts, while expansionary fiscal policy could lead to an earlier-than- expected end to the current easing cycle. All in all, we think the bar for rate hikes remains high, but that would be most likely in the tail-risk scenario described above. 513/02/2026 Pay September MPC, stay long EURGBP

Indeed, as Figure 3 shows, net demand for OATs from French insurers has turned positive since Q2 24, contrasting with the preceding era of steady net sales. In our view, rebounding insurer demand likely in part reflects the recent cessation of outflows from French life insurance products, particularly traditional fonds euros products (which offer relatively heavier exposure to fixed income, versus the relatively greater equity exposure offered by unit- linked products). Indeed, 2025 was the first year since the pandemic that fonds euros products saw positive net inflows ( Figure 4), in contrast to the continual outflows these products saw over 2020-24 (in turn encouraging insurers to sell down OAT holdings). Rather than conclude that the link between sentiment and growth has broken, recent performance should be seen in the nuanced light of multiple behavioral impulses. Rising optimism around new technologies has generated a surge in global tech spending, while business caution around US poli- cy weighs on non-tech spending. Both caution and AI diffu- sion play a role in the job creation stall across the globe. That these behavioral shifts align with solid global GDP growth does not, however, reflect a large tech contribution to global growth. Outside Asia, the tech sector’s growth contribution remains small. Clearing of UST repo is expected to pick up over the coming months as we approach the mandatory deadline. While the official cutoff is Jun-27 (the original Jun-26 deadline was extended last February), most market participants are likely to transition to cleared repo around 3 to 6 months before the deadline. We have received questions on how this shift will affect SOFR fixings; below we estimate the effect of this shift for an array of potential outcomes. As a reminder, SOFR is a volume-weighted median based on tri-party, GCF, and cleared bilateral transactions. The distribution is bimodal, with most cash lending occurring at tri-party and borrowing closer to the SOFR 75th percentile (Figure 12). SOFR fixings tend to move closer to the higher mode on supply dates and quarter- end days (‘bad days’); Figure 13 shows this widening at quarter-end dates. We have discussed before that the quarter-end widening is largely driven by foreign dealers stepping back from repo markets at these dates. This widening tends to increase the dispersion of the SOFR distribution; we show the contrast between a ‘bad day’ (yellow distribution), and a ‘good day’ (blue distribution) in Figure 14. Figure 12. For the Fed, one option could be to have the Treasury Secretary or Interagency Working Group on Treasury Market Surveillance (IAWG) recommend interventions, to the extent timing allows, and/or have the FOMC commit ex ante to sell the acquired securities ba ck. Alternatively, intervention could in effect be done by Treasury, with it issuing bills to conduct buybacks and the Fed in turn buying bills in the open market. With this the Fed would be providing funding liquidity that Treasury uses to support market liquidity. A downside is that it could be cumbersome in environments where speed and flexibility are essential. Reserve-management purchases Last December the Fed began reserve-management purchases (RMPs) to rebuild reserves and eventually increase them in line with demand. Any policy measures that result in a smaller or more slowly growing Fed balance sheet would also lessen the need for RMPs, and any shift in the target steady -state Treasury portfolio could alter their composition. We close our SIGB 10s30s flattener trade idea (see EM rates: Enter a 10s30s SIGB flattener, dated 26 September) for a 16.5bp loss, as it has reached our stop. We initiated the position after the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s 50y SIGB auction in September. Seasonality analysis suggested that the long-end part of the SIGB curve could flatten, as MAS usually doesn’t auction super-long bonds in Q4 and Q1. While the curve flattened somewhat heading into the auction and in the days after, the broader flattening move in 10s30s did not play out as we had expected (see Figure 1). As such, we close our position (long 30y SIGB 3.25% June 2054 and short 10y SIGB 2.75% March 2035) at 27.5bp for a 16.5bp loss (USD330k).

The stronger-than- expected fundamental recovery and breakthroughs similar to the ‘DeepSeek moment’ (a Chinese AI model launched in early 2025 that matched top-tier global modes at low costs) across industries might ignite investor optimism. Anti-involution: In 2026, China will continue to implement anti-involution measures to control overcapacity and foster rational competition. We expect the current soft-policy approach to countering supply-side involution and boosting demand to alleviate but not end entrenched industrial deflation. That said, the sharp rise in commodity prices might allow up/midstream companies to pass through additional cost to their customers. The regime shift is rhetorical, not legislative, but that has been enough for a market that moves on reflexivity, which does not need implemented policy change to sell off but only needs credible political willingness to consider weakening the EU ETS — The EU ETS fundamentals haven’t budged: the inertia of the legislative process at EU level blocks any meaningful change for 2026 and for most of 2027, and our ~200Mt annual deficits for those years are structurally as tight as ever. Yet the tape has decoupled entirely from fundamentals. This is reflexivity at work: Market participants do not appear to price current reality, but instead are pricing what appears true to the majority, and that appearance then becomes self- reinforcing reality through collective behavior. Here, the dominant perception has shifted decisively: Markets consider EU ETS weakening as no longer mere speculation but a credible, discussable policy option at the very core of the EU. Once that belief takes hold, it drives action, compliance buyers pause hedging, “Why front-run if relief looks plausible?”, speculative longs derisk aggressively, which pushes prices lower, which strengthens the perception that “something must be coming, ” which triggers more selling. The loop feeds itself until the flush exhausts or a counter-narrative emerges. records.text: US Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 5 generally thinks the framework has served it well, allowing for effective and efficient control of the fed funds rate. Moving back to a corridor system is possible but the road to that could be long. If the Fed retains ample reserves, as we learned from funding market pressures observed late last year, it cannot let reserves fall from current levels without risking significant upward pressure on the fed funds rate. That is, unless it can reduce bank demand for reserves. The path to lower reserves demand would come primarily via regulatory changes. Two options that come to mind would be relaxing the liquidity coverage ratio or internal liquidity stress test requirements so that banks demand fewer cash assets. In line with this train of thought, Governors Bowman and Miran have recently argued that the Fed’s balance sheet is “downstream of bank regulations.” We expect to hear more on this theme in coming months. The Fed could also reduce total assets without lowering reserves if its other liabilities were to decline. To this end, w hile currency can be thought of as exogenous ly determined, Treasury could run a lower TGA balance or the Fed could restrict or disincentivize usage of the foreign repo pool (i.e., ONRRP for foreign central banks), which has a current balance of around $320bn. The probability distribution of the terminal rate pricing derived from 2y forward 3m swaptions had shown a rightward shift (higher rate expectations) and a wider dispersion (greater uncertainty) since late November, but these movements have largely stalled as markets increasingly priced in a landslide LDP victory in the election ( Figure 10). Looking ahead, we expect developments to be driven less by term premiums and more by increases in the risk‑neutral yield as BoJ rate hikes actually materialize. We have brought forward our expected timing of BoJ rate hikes and raised our terminal rate forecast from 1.25% to 1.50%. While this revision alone would push the 10y risk‑neutral yield (RNY) up by roughly 20bp, we have also taken into account offsetting downward pressures from a pullback in fiscal concerns and terminal rate uncertainty. Weaker USD: Concerns about the credibility of US institutions implies a large, and growing, downside tail for the USD. The Fed’s independent operation has been a necessary condition for the USD to enjoy its status as the global reserve currency and thus reap the benefits of its ‘exorbitant privilege’. Foreign investors hold significant amounts of US assets (Figure 3), and if confidence in US monetary authorities were to be lost, we would anticipate a rapid hedging or selling of these securities. Institutional credibility in FX can be large. EURUSD traded almost 4 standard deviations rich to our short-term fair model estimates after President Trump first proposed firing Chair Powell last year. If the Fed’s independence is indeed seen as compromised, and USD reserve status questioned, USD weakness could be very material. Should the Fed set policy inappropriately loose, we see scope for inflation expectations to de-anchor. This de-anchoring of inflation expectations would erode the competitiveness of the US, which would in turn put sizeable downward pressure on the valuation of the greenback. Higher inflation uncertainty has also historically driven FX volatility higher too.

records.text: With Italy hosting the Winter Olympics over February, we assess the possible impact of increased hospitality demand on overall services activity. Past episodes suggest that major sporting events hosted in Europe raised the level of the services PMI by around 0.5 standard deviations (or around 2pt) above the previous 6-month run rate, with significant variation around this central estimate. That said, Winter Olympics appear to have generated a smaller boost than other events, such as Summer Olympics and FIFA World Cups. In the previous Winter Olympics hosted by Italy in 2006, the services PMI rose by 1.7pt in February, although hard data on tourism showed no meaningful effect (Exhibit 2). We thus upgrade our model-implied forecast for the services PMI in the periphery very modestly this month. records.text: Leadership challenge, resignation or snap election: Shifting voter preferences and heightened tensions between Labour MPs and the Cabinet Office have increased the risk of a change in leadership. The 7 May elections for English local governments and the national parliaments of Scotland and Wales represent the Labour Party’s first key electoral test since the 2024 general election and a key potential catalyst. If the results bear out Labour’s recent weakness in opinion polls (Figure 2), this could lead to renewed calls for a change in party leadership, the resignation of the prime minister, or a snap general election. Given recent news flow, this might happen before May. Any of those scenarios might result in a reassessment of fiscal policy and a move away from fiscal prudence, culminating in an event similar to September 2022. It is such a significant change in fiscal policy that we consider the grey swan; a change in leadership alone would not necessarily lead to a move away from fiscal prudence. In most scenarios, we think a shift in policy composition – more tax and more spend – is more likely than looser policy on aggregate. Potential timeline: Below is how the tail risk of a shift to a less fiscally prudent government might unfold, focused around the May elections. While dissent frequencies vary by country, they have recently become a more notable feature of central bank meetings (left chart, Exhibit 1). The BoE has particularly high levels of disagreement—there has been at least one dissent at each meeting since 2022 (right chart, Exhibit 1) and decisions are often reached by narrow majorities (such as 5-4 at last week’s meeting)—while the FOMC has seen a string of dissents for the first time since late 2005. In contrast, Sweden’s Riksbank has only seen two dissents since 2022. What makes dissents more likely? We collect a cross-country panel of detailed voting data for the ten economies shown in Exhibit 1 and regress a binary dissent indicator on economic data and other policy factors that might predict dissents (while controlling for central bank fixed effects). Dissents are more common following large deviations in inflation from the central bank’s target. A 1pp increase in the core inflation gap raises the likelihood of dissent at the subsequent meeting by 6pp when inflation is currently below target and 8pp when it is above (left chart, Exhibit 2). On the other end of the mandate, a 1pp increase in the unemployment gap (defined as the deviation from its ten-year average) raises the likelihood of dissent by 8pp when unemployment is below its long-term average but lowers it by 5pp when it is above the long-term average. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 13 February 2026 3 create winners and losers, the net effect for the economy is supposed to be positive. This means markets price in today higher aggregate profits in the future, boosting valuation of the stock market and real assets in general. This means people with exposure to financial and real assets feel wealthier and increase consumption to smooth out future expected income into the present. The result is another channel that contributes to overheat the economy. K-shaped consumption to become the norm Interestingly, these short-run effects are consistent with the K-shaped type of consumption we are currently observing in the US. Measured labor productivity (that is, output per hour) continues improving since the end of the pandemic and is mostly concentrated in the services sectors rather than manufacturing. Interestingly, real labor income is not growing at the same pace. In other words, productivity gains translate into higher corporate profits. This dynamic implies a higher share of the GDP pie going into corporate profits relative to labor income. This income dynamic is consistent and being reinforced by the rally in financial as well as real assets, which are more concentrated among higher- and middle-income households. Then the K-shaped consumption dynamics emerges. The productivity surge is also consistent with the observed decoupling between the labor market and the demand side of the economy. In terms of time frame, the additional supply through the Flexibility Share leftover could occur via a Delegate Act, while the others would likely need to go through the Ordinary Legislative Procedure. records.text: George Cole +44(20)7552-1214 | george.cole@gs.com Goldman Sachs International Global Markets Daily: Gilts — A Calculated Risk 13 February 2026 | 12:08PM GMT Despite the outperformance of Gilts since September, there has been a rise in n Gilt risk premium since the beginning of the year that has coincided with a rise in political uncertainty. UK term premium has seen the biggest increase (by our estimates) and the 2s10s curve has out-steepened other major bond markets. Relative to previous episodes of a rise in UK country risk, the current moves are n small, and we estimate that the average rise in 10y Gilt yields from bouts of uncertainty is around 30bp. But our analysis suggests that these bouts of uncertainty are typically short-lived, even when they result in a change in policies towards fiscal loosening. To justify a much larger move in Gilts, market expectations would need to shift n towards more fiscal loosening over the medium term, or a rise in inflation. By our estimates, a 1pp increase in the medium-term deficit is worth around 30-40bp higher 10y Gilt yields. Meanwhile, the ongoing decline in macro uncertainty, further disinflation, and n the prospects for more BoE rate cuts all tighten the bounds on potential moves in Gilts. While UK risk premium and political uncertainty will likely remain elevated through upcoming local elections, we think the favourable macro backdrop will drive Gilt yields lower, and we continue to forecast 10y Gilts at 4.0% at end-2026. records.text: GSE update on interest rate risk hedging policies Since President Trump's announcement earlier in the year that he was authorizing Freddie and Fannie to purchase $200bn in MBS in an effort to lower mortgage rates, market participants have been wondering how the hedging footprint would be felt in the rates market. We had quantified the potential hedging needs that could arise in this piece. While the duration hedging needs are manageable, the theoretical vol hedging needs could vastly exceed swaption market supply, so even fractional hedging of vol would be significant. Freddie and Fannie retained portfolios had already risen significantly in the second half of last year—it is not clear if the $200bn announced by President Trump includes these quantities or not. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 13/02/2026 06:20:52 GMT Distributed on: 13/02/2026 06:20:52 GMT 13 February 2026 Chart of the week: Record FDI income and challenges for fund repatriation Balance of payment statistics for 2025, released on 9 February, show that income from Japan’s outward foreign direct investment (FDI) came to ¥31.7trn for the year, setting a fourth consecutive record high. This figure reflects the acceleration in overseas investment by Japanese businesses in recent years, which has grown 2.7 times since 2015 and 8.1 times since 2005. However, a a significant portion of this income – ¥13.1trn, or 41.3% – was reinvested earnings, meaning the profits were retained by overseas subsidiaries for business expansion and other purposes rather than being repatriated to Japan as dividends. That is, slightly less than 60% of the profits earned overseas was repatriated to Japan in the form of dividends or interest. If the ratio of reinvested earnings could be reduced and the repatriation of capital increased, it could achieve two key objectiv es. First, it could ease the selling pressure on the yen driven by actual demand, one of the factors behind the yen’s depreciation in recent years. Second, it could provide a new source of funds for domestic investment, a priority topic for Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Key Takeaways Our equity analysts revise higher their outlook for Hyperscaler capex in 2026 and 2027. We raise our estimate of growth in nonresidential business fixed investment and imports. We now expect real GDP growth of 2.6% in 2026, up from 2.4% previously. Revisions to payrolls point to faster growth in productivity. We estimate the y/y change in productivity through 3Q 25 at 2.4%, vs 1.9% as currently reported. We also see the source of downside risk to the economy as shifting from trade protectionism to an asset-investment boom-bust cycle. The data has elements of a demand-driven and supply-driven boost to the economy. Where inflation and unemployment goes depends on which one wins out. While TJX has historically been the more consistent comp grower, we are excited about ROST’s comp momentum and outsized margin opportunity. We could see further multiple convergence if ROST continues to deliver consistent comps. Card data points to deceleration in spending post-holiday Discount apparel spending increased 2% in 4Q, accelerating from flat in 3Q, according to BAC aggregated credit and debit card data. This includes a deceleration in January, driven by the storm which hurt the weeks ended Jan 24th and Jan 31st. Overall for those weeks, B&M retailers saw a deceleration across categories, including discount, while e- commerce accelerated. Interestingly, spending growth by lower income cohorts on discount apparel outpaced that of higher income cohorts (which declined) in January. Sales driven by AUR rather than transaction volume Discount spending over the last few months has been driven primarily by higher transaction values as transaction volumes have been flat or declining (Exhibits 1, 2). While higher transaction values could be partly due to a mix shift towards higher AUR items, we view the increase in ATVs as evidence that discount retailers are raising prices. Consumer staples have outperformed the SPX by around 10% over a month—something extremely rare outside of a strong down market. Backtesting this event (with a condition that the SPX is still above the 55ma when a 7% outperformance of staples triggers), we only found five previous events since 1998. Those were April and July of 2000, January and April of 2022, and February of 2025, all moments that were followed by some market softness, as per Figure 6. While it may appear strange that cyclicals are also doing well, this is actually not so rare during those events, as per Figure 7. records.text: he initial catalyst is different and the timeline accelerates, the process would look similar. ▪ 7 May: Elections bear out Labour’s weakness in opinion polls. ▪ Mid/late May: Prime Minister Keir Starmer faces a leadership challenge, resigns or calls an early general election. ▪ Early/mid-summer: After a multi-week process, there is a change in the country’s leadership. A leadership contest for the Labour Party typically takes six to eight weeks, while a snap election takes at least 25 working days between the dissolution of Parliament and polling day. ▪ Late September and early October: Party conferences and cabinet reshuffles signal policy shifts, creating scope for volatility. ▪ Mid/late autumn: The budget includes fiscal policy announcements. Budgets have historically taken place six to nine weeks after polling day, but including Office for Budget Responsibility projections would require 10 weeks’ notice. Composition matters: On budget day, markets scrutinise not only the size of any fiscal expansion but also its composition. For instance, higher investment spending might be seen as more credible than unfunded tax cuts, higher welfare spending, or stopping interest payments on central bank reserves. Moreover, policy changes can create relative winners and losers in credit or equities. This is where decomposing rates into their fundamental drivers becomes a useful framework of analysis. Figure 3 shows a modeled decomposition of 10y gilt yields broken down into its two key drivers: the expectation component and the term premium component. The former has been declining as the rate cycle has matured, so it has been the elevated level of term premium that has kept 10y rates higher. This is significant, since if the expectation component is stabilising, variations in term premium will be the dominant driver of changes in 10y rates. While the tendency for US CPI to surprise to the upside in January is well documented, it is a trend that has nevertheless proved persistent, both relative to the economists’ consensus and relative to inflation market pricing. Compared to the economists’ consensus compiled by Bloomberg, January core CPI has surprised to the upside in ten out of the past eleven years (Figure left); the average (median) forecast error has been 9bp (11bp) over that period. 2014 was the last ‘in-line’ release (defined as a deviation of less than 5bp from the two-decimal average consensus), while pandemic-era 2021 surprised to the downside. Similarly, the January CPI print has come out above the inflation market fixing in ten out of the past eleven years (2021 again being the exception; Figure right), with an average (median) beat of 14bp (16bp). We count on lower US rates, perhaps alongside higher Fed independence risks, China stimulus, strong FX hedging activity, and a somewhat lower bar for upside surprises in Europe vs mid-2025. Valuation keeps us cautious on CHF, but it can get supported by elevated geopolitical and/or fiscal concerns. EM Structurally we maintain the constructive stance on EM which we have held since January. The BofA baseline envisages a weaker USD; lower rates; low oil pr ices; and moderately higher equities. records.text: Global Research Highlights | 13 February 2026 9 Global Research Marketing 10 Micro Themes for 2026: Acquisitions and AI are just the beginning 1) M&A likely to reach record levels M&A activity is set to accelerate, supported by regulatory change, stable rates, and pent‑up demand. These conditions point to a sustained deal cycle into 2026, benefiting industries from biotech to banks to media to M&A advisors. 2) AI buildout is mid-cycle, some valuations compelling Vivek Arya believes we are in the mid‑cycle of a multi‑year AI buildout. Semiconductors are tracking ~30% growth in 2026. Certain semi valuations look attractive versus growth. Accelerating enterprise, sovereign, and cloud adoption reinforce the trajectory. 3) Industrial momentum improving U.S. manufacturing is returning to expansion, short‑cycle demand is accelerating. Ongoing capex, reshoring, easier credit conditions support an earnings‑driven upswing. 4) Defense spend could step higher in 2026 Global defense spending is entering a sustained upcycle toward 2030, driven by geopolitics and higher NATO budgets. Large defense primes could benefit. 5) GLP1 access to broaden, impacting various groups Lower GLP-1 prices and orals may negatively impact PBMs, could pressure snack/alcohol volumes too. Within restaurants, QSRs more at risk given higher mix of snacking. 6) Higher tax refunds support some consumer stocks in 1Q Tax season stimulus is expected to average ~$1,000 per household, providing a near‑term boost to GDP.

Financial markets react in manners directionally consistent with the policy signal from dissents, with a hawkish dissent from 10% of the committee raising expected short rates by 0.7bp and lowering equity prices by 8bp. Canary on the Committee? Interest rate and monetary policy decisions are made via committee in virtually all global central banks, and most reveal voting outcomes to the public. In this Global Economics Comment, we examine the historical voting records of ten major global central banks to assess the sources of, and signals from, monetary policy dissents. Global central banks take different approaches to the tradeoff between promoting transparency and fostering committee cohesion. Several central banks, including the Fed and BoE, report individual voting outcomes. Several others report aggregate, unattributed vote totals (RBA, RBNZ) or comment on whether the decision was unanimous (ECB). In contrast, the BoC does not conduct a formal vote and follows a consensus approach where all members must agree on the policy decision. However, the diversification of China's holdings - both private and official - away from US assets has been evident in the data for a while. The share of USD bonds in China banks' external portfolio for instance already fell markedly in 2025 (see report: China banks’ exposure to USD bonds 13 February 2026). In terms of fresh structural USD selling, the focus should be on Europe where holdings are concentrated in equities with lower hedge ratios. Equity flows do not yet suggest a rush for the exit, but it seems likely that incremental flow will head more to non-US markets over time, in addition to the risk of higher hedge ratios ( FX Viewpoint 12 February 2026). The Fed, as an institution, depends on congressional and public confidence and support in its goals, strategy and operating framework, and this support could prove elusive in the coming year as both political parties compete for votes among lower-income consumers. Moreover, we believe many FOMC policymakers are only loosely personally committed to the 2% inflation goal; under Powell’s tenure as Chair, policymakers have asterisked this goal in a variety of different ways, such as by making it into an average, an underlying trend, a range, or a long-term expectation. Indeed, January inflation eased some concerns about a repricing of services at the start of the year, which is also improving the outlook for policy easing after the elections. The post-election outlook: We would expect a Tisza victory alongside a stronger forint to make it more comfortable for the NBH to cut rates further – and give us more confidence in our forecast for disinflation in 2026. We think a drop in Hungarian inflation is sustainable and following a deceleration at the start of the year, it is likely to remain close to the NBH’s 3.0% inflation target (Figure 8), even with less favourable base effects kicking in in Q2 2026 and the prospect of an unwind of government price control measures after the elections. We would also be more inclined to lower our current end- 2026 policy rate forecast of 5.50% and bring forward our 4.75% terminal policy rate to early 2027 from H2 2027. In contrast, a status quo in government, or a spike in political and economic uncertainty (and government instability) is likely to be more challenging for a central bank which remains highly sensitive to HUF performance. We do not think any election outcome prevents the NBH from cutting rates towards 5.5% after the election, but it could make the path to policy rate normalisation bumpier. 413/02/2026 Policy ramification

Page 20 EUR STIR: Basis surprises again Soniya Sadeesh | Strategist | +44-20-754-73091 Note: This note was originally published on 10 February 2026. The recent decline in 3M Euribor fixings has been a source of questions. Today's FICOTD shows both the spread of fixings versus OIS and commercial paper versus OIS across the 3M, 6M and 12M tenors. It can be seen that commercial paper is a decent anchor point for 6M and 12M fixing s, but less so for the 3M. More recently the gap is particularly stark for both the 3M and 6M sectors. Without granular data to cover the entire transaction base, explaining these dynamics is near impossible, short of anecdotes. We would expect this to correct, as has been the case in the past. We continue to make the case that with ongoing QT and limited usage of the ECB facilities, the liquidity backdrop remains one in which conditions should tighten ( even if it is gradual). d consumer pocketbooks and reduced spending, weighted on corporate margins and business spending, and reversed asset market gains. Looking ahead, and in light of revisions toward our upside scenarios alongside buoyant risk assets, the source of downside risk is likely shifting. The more an AI-related capex cycle drives growth in economic activity, the greater the risk that it poses from an overinvestment cycle should investment returns not materialize. At least that is what history suggests; all major innovation cycles have come with credit cycles and boom-bust characteristics. And as consumption levels have been overshooting model-implied target levels, there are also risks for upper-income cohorts pulling back in case of large and persistent asset market volatility. If so, the deflating of an asset-investment bubble will pose ever greater risk to the economy over our forecast horizon than the effective tariff rate. For now, we leave our downside scenario as is given the uncertainty around the forthcoming Supreme Court decision on the validity of IEEPA tariffs and forthcoming USMCA review, but our views on downside risks to the economy are evolving.

If reallocated 100%, there should be no overall arithmetic change to the RIN supply- demand balance, as larger refiners would have greater obligations to offset SREs. Tuck-in acquisitions create business mix uncertainty We believe that A.I. disintermediation is largely a risk exclusive to personal lines and small commercial policies. Companies that do dozens of tuck-in acquisitions annually are picking up a hodge-podge of sophisticated business as well as personal lines and small commercial. While we expect the vast majority of the business at large public agents and brokers is not subject to disintermediation, a non-immaterial slice may be. Insurance broker disclosure is too thin to allow investors to make an educated decision regarding the proportion of revenues that might face some risk. Fortune 500 not buying insurance from a chat-bot We do believe that large account Fortune 500 business is largely immune from this type of disintermediation. records.text: ptions: Rising noise amid anchored realized vol In the front end, a weak GDP print reinforced the dovish MPC surprise from last week and kept a March rate cut in play, yet front‑end implied vol has not risen much. With UK inflation still above target, the BoE has ample time to reassess policy after each cut, as a result of which the forward rate beyond Q3 26 has been insulated from near‑term noise. On the other hand, the long end is more exposed to noise, as the risk of a potential leadership challenge triggered a short‑lived 7bp/y rise in GBP long‑end implied vol from its 60bp/y lows. This move retraced quickly, but the episode exposed the fragility of the UK long end, which will remain subject to headline sensitivity into the May local elections. GBP long-end implied vol continues to look rich against historically low realized vol With this uptick in implied vol, the implied vs realised gap in the UK long end has widened again ( Figure 5). The pickup in vol risk premium has risen alongside payer skew, reflecting growing fiscal unease. Yet these premia have not been validated by realised volatility, as underlying price action remains muted. Realised volatility in the UK has remained anchored near two‑decade lows, only marginally above the stability seen in 2005–06. The triparty repo rate (TGCR) has moved from trading persistently above interest on reserve balances (IORB) at the end of last year to slightly below it. The effective fed funds rate (EFFR), the more stable of the two, has anchored itself at 1 bps below IORB after climbing rapidly from 7 bps below. The broad trend in these two money market rates could be particularly helpful for identifying major shifts in reserve conditions, as shown in today’s chart. This is a good indication that the Fed’s reserve management purchases (RMPs) are working to stabilize money market conditions. Other factors may have also contributed, such as seasonal bill paydowns from December through mid - January and dealer balance shee t redeployment after the year -end. Less attractive Treasury basis opportunities may also have reduced the demand for repo. However, these dynamics are fluid. Bill supply is on the rise again, and dealers could tighten balance sheets if they run into leverage constraints. Looking ahead, reserve management purchases are likely to continue at their current pace into the spring. records.text: FX Strategy: Broad JPY strength on the “Takaichi rally” Shinichiro Kadota BSJL, Japan | Lhamsuren Sharavdemberel BSJL, Japan This week, following the landslide victory of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) in Sunday’s lower house election, the JPY initially weakened modestly before drawing buyers as concerns over fiscal deterioration receded and repeated verbal intervention by government officials supported the currency. Japanese assets saw a “triple gain” of higher equities, lower JGB yields and a stronger JPY. After the election, USDJPY rose from around 157 to the high-157s at one point, but subsequently declined amid continued JPY strength, falling to the low‑152s on the 12 th, approaching the post-rate-check lows seen last month. In addition to FM Katayama, Vice FM Mimura has continued to intervene verbally, stating that authorities are “constantly communicating with markets, ” “closely monitoring markets with a high sense of urgency” (on the 9th), and that they are “not letting down their guard at all” (on the 12th, Bloomberg). These remarks have also provided support for the JPY. That said, while the JPY has appreciated recently, we do not believe this marks a structural shift toward a stronger‑JPY trend. Rate differentials, persistently elevated overseas investment and Japan’s digital trade deficit remain factors weighing on the JPY. JGB yields no longer low: For decades, Japanese investors have avoided low- yield JGBs and kept foreign bonds as a core investment to enhance yields. However, that trend is beginning to shift. The 10y JGB yield is now approaching the 10y Bund yield, which makes JGB 10y is attractive compared with FX-hedged foreign sovereign bonds, and the 10s30s is steeper than other G4 sovereign bonds (Figure 1). Because of high uncertainty around the BoJ’s terminal rate, it is difficult to gauge where yields will stop rising, but once the terminal rate becomes clear and a buying case for JGBs emerges, we can expect a reallocation toward JGB-centric portfolios. When that happens, Japanese investors’ rationale for continuing to hold foreign bonds will weaken. Big impact of regulatory change to flow: To curb excessive rises in bond yields and a weakening JPY, policymakers could introduce regulatory changes aimed at halting capital outflows and steering funds back into domestic investments. Although the ratio rises somewhat during the tax‑cut period due to a decline in nominal GDP – by 0.25pp in FY27, when the tax cut is applied for a full year ( Figure 11) – it returns to a level broadly comparable to the base case (BC) after the tax cut ends. This reflects the containment of adverse effects on both the primary balance and GDP through efficient funding measures. The next‑smallest increase in the debt/GDP ratio occurs under the JGB issuance scenario. Driven mainly by a deterioration in the primary balance, the ratio rises by 1.8pp relative to the base case in FY28 and then remains broadly flat. Although the ratio improves after the tax cut ends, the effects of the tax cut persist, with the debt/GDP ratio remaining about 1.4pp higher than the base case. The scenario in which the debt/GDP ratio deteriorates the most is the cutback of economically important subsidies scenario. Under this scenario, real GDP declines by slightly more than 0.2% relative to the base case during the tax‑cut period and by 0.5% even after the tax cut ends. As a result, the decline in nominal GDP relative to the base case exceeds 0.7%. Consequently, the debt/GDP ratio rises by nearly 2.4pp relative to the base case during the tax‑cut period, with an increase of more than 1.8pp persisting even after the tax cut ends. In this case, debt levels worsen more than under the JGB issuance scenario. 13 February 2026 12 Barclays |

Public experience over decades with an independent Fed has brought about enormous confidence in its long-term success in achieving these goals, enabling low long-term nominal interest rates and stable foreign exchange rates. Goals: An explicit inflation target is a relatively recent innovation in Fed history. It dates only to January 2012 under Chairman Ben Bernanke. The inflation target, by design, limits policymaker discretion by tying the central bank’s credibility to the achievement of 2% inflation over a reasonable period. The FOMC implemented two other transparency mechanisms around the same time to provide discipline and accountability around the 2% inflation goal. First, its Summary of Economic Projections forces the disclosure of an inflation path; its construction nudges officials to calibrate policy so that 2% inflation is achieved within about two years, the length of the projection. Second, post-meeting press conferences force the Chair to regularly explain the policy stance and take public responsibility for policy outcomes. (These processes similarly provide accountability on employment, the other leg of the FOMC’s dual mandate.) Erosion: The White House, so far, seems to have found little traction in driving change at the Fed via personnel turnover. records.text: 3 Most of us spend too little time on the less likely: This is an analysis of tail risks across the global economy and markets: risks that have a seemingly low probability but would have a high impact on growth and markets if they occurred. Tail risks are difficult to manage precisely because they seem so unlikely. They aren’t part of the base-case scenarios to which most people devote most of their time: where is the economy going next year; what will happen to earnings; how central banks will respond; and how much of that’s priced in by markets. Having a well-informed base case is a requirement for anyone hoping to have an edge in investing. But the base case – the centre of the distribution of possible outcomes – is often a crowded space, thoroughly scrutinised, and typically based on scenarios that are known and likely. ‘Known and likely’ move markets, but typically in orderly, moderate ways because they are already anticipated by many. Handling grey swans: The bigger market moves often occur when something previously thought of as unlikely suddenly happens (Figure 1). These ‘grey swans’ – considered possible but unlikely – often have an outsized impact both because they surprise and because few have planned or positioned for them. In our experience, people frequently underestimate the likeliness of unlikely risks. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W Entering pay September MPC: We enter a new trade, as we think the BoE’s hands will be tied until fiscal policy is unveiled, particularly since Bank Rate is approaching the nominal neutral rate range. Since we do not expect any material policy announcements to happen until the autumn budget and continue to think that any leadership contest would be most likely to occur from May onwards, we think the BoE will maintain the status quo over the May–September period. Paying the September MPC meeting also supports our base case, which foresees one more cut this quarter, then a hold for the rest of the year. The main risks to our trade are a decline in political uncertainty, a deterioration of the labour market, and inflation undershooting the target, as these could accelerate the pace of cuts. New trade idea: Pay September MPC. Entry: 3.30%. Target 3.48%. Stop-loss: 3.23bp. Risk: (25k/01). Stay long EURGBP: For FX, we see two channels for our political scenarios to affect the GBP: the rates channel, reflecting the BoE path; and the risk premium channel, reflecting uncertainty around fiscal dynamics. Under Scenario 2 in Figure 5, we see EURGBP rising to 0.92 (+3.5% vs the end-2026 forward). This reflects the scope GBP weakness through the rates channel, but also a risk premium being embedded to reflect protracted uncertainty ahead of an eventual budget. records.text: ts a structural shift for Nigeria’s economy. The country is now a net exporter of refined fuel including petrol, jet fuel, diesel, among others. Exports since 2024 have reached at least $2 billion. Looking ahead, Dangote Industries is positioning itself as a major exporter of refined fuels across Africa and globally, while strengthening Nigeria’s energy security, industrial base, and balance of payments. Fertiliser and gas integration Dangote Industries also operates Africa’s largest fertiliser plant, producing urea using natural gas as feedstock. The fertiliser complex occupies about 500 hectares and supports both domestic supply and exports. Feedstock inputs include nitrogen, hydrogen, and CO₂, reinforcing Nigeria’s agricultural productivity and export potential. Crude for naira sales reduce dollar demand Dangote refineries can fully meet the 300k bpd local needs and still contribute to exports. Some direct arrangements involve FGN through NNPC supplying 12mn barrels of crude oil (390k bpd) to Dangote to be refined and sold in naira as gasoline, diesel and aviation fuels. The deal could save costs for Nigeria and ease dollar demand, thus supporting the naira. Petroleum imports use up to 40% of total FX demand.

A scenario where the Fed reacts to an AI-productivity-created rise in joblessness could trigger a melt higher in equities. Late 1990s playbook: The Fed cut rates in 1998 in response to the Long-Term Capital Management crisis. This was a time when the equity market was already running hot. This preceded one of the largest melts higher for US equities. The S&P 500 rallied 50% in the following year. When the market hit all-time highs in 2000, it was an environment of spot up/vol up. If we were to consider a similar scenario is spot terms from today’s starting levels – it would imply SPX at 10k. From a volatility perspective, longer-dated SPX is not cheap. The response of inflation and employment would depend on the central bank’s choices: inflation temporarily decelerating faster toward 2% before a later rise; and unemployment rising at first, then falling. Modeling shows that the neutral rate of interest (r*), rises on a forward-looking basis to higher expected productivity growth. This means that if AI sentiment becomes more exuberant, monetary policy could become more stimulative, bringing an inflationary cyclical boom on top of productivity-fueled growth. US ECONOMY: AN AI PRODUCTIVITY BOOM Why it’s important: Our base case has been that the transformational effects of AI will come with a significant lag – akin to the 1970s and 1980s, when a surge in IT investment did not boost measured labor productivity until the 1990s. However, if breakneck investment in AI data centers means that those productivity gains come faster, the global economy could undergo a rapid and profound transformation. How it might happen: Firms continue to pour investment into AI-related projects and transform their businesses. US GDP growth skyrockets with moderate inflation, but this amplifies the ‘K-shaped’ economy with some groups of workers losing out. The regime shift is rhetorical, not legislative, but that has been enough for a market that moves on reflexivity, which does not need implemented policy change to sell off but only needs credible political willingness to consider weakening the EU ETS — The EU ETS fundamentals haven’t budged: the inertia of the legislative process at EU level blocks any meaningful change for 2026 and for most of 2027, and our ~200Mt annual deficits for those years are structurally as tight as ever. Yet the tape has decoupled entirely from fundamentals. This is reflexivity at work: Market participants do not appear to price current reality, but instead are pricing what appears true to the majority, and that appearance then becomes self- reinforcing reality through collective behavior. Here, the dominant perception has shifted decisively: Markets consider EU ETS weakening as no longer mere speculation but a credible, discussable policy option at the very core of the EU. Once that belief takes hold, it drives action, compliance buyers pause hedging, “Why front-run if relief looks plausible?”, speculative longs derisk aggressively, which pushes prices lower, which strengthens the perception that “something must be coming, ” which triggers more selling. The loop feeds itself until the flush exhausts or a counter-narrative emerges. While the tendency for US CPI to surprise to the upside in January is well documented, it is a trend that has nevertheless proved persistent, both relative to the economists’ consensus and relative to inflation market pricing. Compared to the economists’ consensus compiled by Bloomberg, January core CPI has surprised to the upside in ten out of the past eleven years (Figure left); the average (median) forecast error has been 9bp (11bp) over that period. 2014 was the last ‘in-line’ release (defined as a deviation of less than 5bp from the two- decimal average consensus), while pandemic -era 2021 surprised to the downside. Similarly, the January CPI print has come out above the inflation market fixing in ten out of the past eleven years (2021 again being the exception; Figure right), with an average (median) beat of 14bp (16bp). From a valuation perspective, the JGB2s30s flattener is the elephant in the bond market room, with a potential 100bp flattening. Real policy rates are too low on an absolute and cross -market basis given the wage dynamics. Long -dated forwards are too high o n a cross -market basis given Japan’s external position. Now that the Japan election is behind us, the question is whether the policy choices of the incoming administration will support the flattening of the curve. Two weeks ago, we argued that the risk-reward was in favour of elephant hunting for two reasons. Firstly, high inflation is unlikely to be politically popular in a nation with significant private sector savings. This is increasingly reflected in opinion polls that have listed cost-of-living as the number one issue for voters by a significant margin. Abenomics 2.0 is therefore unlikely to be politically (let alone economically) sound in such an environment. Secondly, even though the BoJ did not provide a convincing hawkish signal at its last meeting, policymakers have subsequently demonstrated low tolerance for further weakness in currency and bond markets. Most polling margins of error are claimed at between 3.0–3.5%, suggesting that, in the absence of a major shift in party fortunes, Tisza appears to be comfortably in the running to form a stable majority government after 12 April – we think a 4–5pp lead is required. The electoral system: Hungary, as part of the EU, runs a party-list proportional, single-round election system every four years. For Hungarian residents, this is based on a two-vote (individual candidate and national list), mixed-member majoritarian representation on a ‘first- past-the-post’ basis (i.e. the winning candidate does not have to get an absolute majority). This means that of the 199 members of parliament – 106 are elected through individual constituencies and the remainder via national list seats. Parties can only take up national list seats if they meet a 5% electoral threshold. Election timeline: Political parties will kick off their official campaigns in the coming week, with the deadlines to register individual candidates and national parties on 6 and 7 March respectively. We would now expect to see the inclusion of more detail around election manifestos. Once votes are tallied on 12 April, Hungary’s constitution stipulates that the formation of the new National Assembly – and the appointment of a prime minister – must take place no later than 12 May, i.e. within one month of the election. records.text: ublic credit markets: A private credit liquidity crunch and rise in defaults could spill over into public credit markets, as investors assign a higher default risk premium for lower-rated credits, especially to small and medium-sized enterprises with floating-rate debt outstanding in a tech-adjacent sector (i.e. leveraged loans). We also see public credit markets as potentially vulnerable to selling pressure, should investors take losses on locked-up private credit portfolios and instead opt to sell more liquid holdings to raise cash. Private credit CLOs: We believe private credit CLOs could be vulnerable to selling pressure if downgrade pressures rise. The private credit CLO market has expanded significantly over the last three years, from about USD80bn in early 2022 to about USD200bn currently. Private credit CLOs tend to include larger ‘CCC’ loan baskets than standard CLOs (~9% versus ~4% on average). The immediate impact of a drop private credit loan valuations would be greater haircuts applied to excess ‘CCC’ and defaulted loans, leading to a deterioration in CLO coverage tests. Also, CLO tranches would be directly affected by a severe private credit default cycle. Assuming a 50% recovery rate, it would take at least about a 20% annual default rate (over the next few years) to incur some principal loss on a private credit CLO ‘BBB’ tranche, which is an extremely remote scenario. Will this translate into lower inflation? The evidence on this point is less clear, because technological improvements create significant change in relative prices, particularly the price of goods vs services. If some prices fall because of AI-driven lower costs of production, the improvement in purchasing power can be used to buy other goods and services, which might not have benefited from the tech boom and/or whose supply is more inelastic. That means in equilibrium higher prices for those goods and services, dampening the disinflationary effects of the technological improvements in the first place. A good example of this is China entering WTO while increasing the supply of labor as well as incorporating new technologies to produce goods that are very low cost and effectively export deflation in goods to the rest of the world. Even though the US imported deflation in goods from China, overall inflation remained around 2% because the income effect of lower goods prices was spent in services and service inflation remained well above the 2% target over those years. records.text: 6 Europe Economic Weekly | 13 February 2026 Of course, wage growth without a glimpse at productivity growth would be misleading. The focus on the drop in French labour productivity measures after Covid has vanished and perhaps for obvious reasons: the gap to Euro area productivity levels, at least vs 2019 reference points, has closed. There was a case to be made during that period that the significant rise in labour force participation and employment ratios in France pushed people into the labour market that previously weren’t. While labour productivity in conventional terms has suffered that, productivity of the total working age population (or, indeed, labour market potential) has significantly improved, a point forcefully made by Banque de France a couple of years ago. 2 And perhaps, as that process is slowing, “on-the-job productivity” improvements dominate again. In fact, since mid-24, France reports labour productivity growth close to two times its 2000-19 average, albeit from very low starting points (Exhibit 5). The economy-wide disinflation effect therefore works simultaneously through two channels: lower nominal wage growth and higher productivity growth. records.text: roduce real spending figures. The data show that growth in real retail sales ex autos has been broadly similar across income groups in the last one to two years. This is, of course, just one data source, and some other sources have shown underperformance for low-income households recent- ly. In addition, the Numerator data does show low-income groups underperformed in earlier years, leading to weaker cumulative spending growth since 2022. Nonetheless, it high- lights that direct measures of spending don’t uniformly sug- gest high-income spending growth has recently been pulling away. Information about the Numerator panel and its correlation to the Census Bureau’s retail sales report can be found in this 2024 FEDS note. The panel has 200,000 households who self-report household income and are encouraged to submit physical and digital spending receipts via an app for everyone in the household. Spending cuts by income are available for income less than $40k, $40-$125k, and greater than $125k. Based on Census income figures, the $40k cutoff would be between the 20th and 30th percentile of household income, and $125k between the 60th and 70th percentile. It is possible that panels like this undersample the extreme high end of the income distribution. In December, real low-income spending rose 2.7%oya vs. 0.5-0.6% for middle- and high-income households, but monthly figures are volatile and the thing that stands out is that growth rates have been similar in the last year (Figure 1).
