records.text: ucky that French fiscal couldn’t correct? Looking closely at the French economy, we draw three main conclusions. First, if growth has held up better than expected, especially since the home-made 2024 policy uncertainty shock, prices have taken the hit and reflect the weakness that growth didn’t. Second, if the ECB considers itself in a “good place” for the Euro area on aggregate (and regulars know we don’t agree), France cannot be in a good place with such price dynamics. Monetary policy is too tight. That’s the relic of the powerful and swift (and we thought correct) French response to the energy crises that capped energy prices and thereby lowered the inflation peak. Third, public finances don’t look great, but the absence of corrective action may have accidentally preserved the economy from a particularly sour policy mix. Of course, a 5% deficit doesn’t look sustainable, even less so if nominal growth is weaker than it should be. Corrective action will be extra tough – political majorities are one thing, but avoiding extra-large fiscal multipliers when monetary policy is tight adds to the challenge.

records.text: ould the Fed want to shrink the balance sheet significantly, it would need to work to reduce banks' demand for reserves. Barring that and shrinking the balance sheet, the Fed might find itself suddenly on the steep part of the reserve demand curve without much warning should it push things too far, which is a risk, given the difficulty in sketching this demand out with precision ( Figure 3). The Fed could rely on the standing repo operations (SRP) to hold rates in check, but this is a risky proposition, given the SRP limitations that came to light in Q4 25 such as banks' hesitance to use it due to the perceived stigma. Moreover, given that leverage demand has grown substantially over the years, the amount of collateral financing in overnight funding markets is quite high, so such a spike could spark a disorderly unwinding of these positions. This would be counterproductive to the goal of shrinking the balance sheet, as the Fed would likely be forced to step in and buy USTs, as it did in March 2020. records.text: Our thoughts on JPY, USD, AUD, EUR, GBP , HUF, MYR, & The Dollar and the Software Sell-off JPY: Too much too soon. The LDP’s landslide victory in the Lower House election n has strikingly sparked a different market response than going into the event. In the weeks leading up to the snap election, as the odds increased of PM Takaichi achieving a broader mandate, long-end yields rose and the currency weakened— consistent with the inflationary backdrop implied by greater fiscal stimulus and constrained monetary policy, as we outlined in our framework for JGBs and JPY. But in the days since, the 5s30s curve has flattened, traded inflation is stable, and the Yen has strengthened, as the market is now pricing some higher likelihood of shifting portfolio flows and an exit from the exceptionally low real rate regime. That leaves a dovish BoJ the main risk in the near term that could revive the prior dynamic, and we have highlighted institutional challenges that will likely make this turn more difficult in Japan. While current conditions can probably run further given the balance of risks and momentum into a vacuum over the next few weeks, our bias is that this is potentially “too much too soon,” with a return of JPY weakening and long-end rate volatility likely to follow if the BoJ were to use recent Yen strength to stay on a more gradual hiking path. Primary metals production picked up strongly through 2025 as tariffs were introduced; it then fell sharply in Novem- ber but rebounded in December. Aerospace has been chugging upward since the post-strike recovery at Boeing, and given the recent surge in orders, out- put is likely to remain resilient for the coming months. In contrast, consumer durables has been in a downward spiral since 2022, ticking down by another 0.7% m/m in December. The public finance trajectory looks uncomfortable, and meaningful correction any time soon looks unlikely. But for the economy, that may have avoided a particularly sour policy mix. We reiterate our growth forecast at 1.1% for 2026 and 1.3% in 2027, a tad below the Euro area. We take out ETS2 from the inflation forecast (done for the Euro area earlier this year) and now see French HICP inflation at 1.3% in 2026 (unch) and 1.5% in 2027 (- 20bp) vs the Euro area at 1.7% in both years. The risk balance is extra wonky in France, in our view. The 2027 presidential election is a potential source for a renewed Economic Policy Uncertainty shock, when the economy just digested the 2024 one. Low inflation may have helped external competitiveness, but the strong EUR may offset that effect and add to domestic disinflation pressures. Public finances are on a very uncomfortable trajectory, and lower nominal growth from low inflation will not make it easier. ECB cuts in 2027 should help, but policy will likely remain tighter in France, especially if majorities for fiscal corrections can be found again post-elections (our base case is built on status quo). The main beneficiary would likely be China, given it has a vote share of only just over 6% despite being the world’s second largest economy (Figure 3). records.text: in at 5.2%. We see a modest decline in vacancies and flat HMRC payrolls, with downside risks around both of these forecasts. Overall, labour demand remains lacklustre, and the build-up of slack has dampened pay pressures. We expect private sector regular pay growth to slide to 3.4% 3M/Y in 4Q25, in line with the BoE. From here on out, the pace of pay disinflation slows – but we think it hovers around target-consistent levels through 2026. On the inflation front, we see headline and core at 10bp higher than the BoE. It's important not to lose sight of the fact that this would still be a decent decline in headline inflation – the first step towards 2%Y, which we think will be attained in April – but we accept that investors are by and large focused on the delta versus the BoE. Given our labour market forecasts, we think that a 10bp beat in inflation that we are expecting won't suffice to prevent a March cut, which is our base case. Given weight- and catering discounting-related noise in this print, we do think that a serious beat in inflation is needed to bring a March cut more into question – in the area of 3.3%Y or, of course, higher – where such a print would not even yield any meaningful disinflation. records.text: Since October, the main drivers of Gilt yields have been the shift towards more dovish policy outcomes (captured in our framework above) and the sharp decline in WAM, resulting in a drought for long-end Gilt issuance (Exhibit 5). According to our macro models, around 10bp of the decline in 30y Gilt yields over that period cannot be explained by macro factors, suggesting a role for supply reductions. This has corresponded to an underperformance of 10y rates on the curve since the November budget, with 30y rates outperforming the usual beta to front-end yields (Exhibit 6). That said, 10y Gilts (and other curve points) have performed well vs swaps, suggesting WAM reduction has boosted Gilts vs other forms of duration. From here however, we think that further significant WAM reductions are unlikely, even with the possibility of higher bill issuance following the DMO’s consultation. Instead, we think that the underlying reduction in macro volatility will support Gilts. Forecast dispersion in inflation and growth is not at pre-pandemic lows, but has settled into a much lower range (Exhibit 7). And further disinflation and BoE cuts, as forecast by our economists, should fundamentally constrain the outcome for Gilts this year. Finally, with volatility adjusted carry now back to multi-year highs (Exhibit 8), we expect Gilts to offer not only good carry but strong price appreciation over the year. For the Fed, one option could be to have the Treasury Secretary or Interagency Working Group on Treasury Market Surveillance (IAWG) recommend interventions, to the extent timing allows, and/or have the FOMC commit ex ante to sell the acquired securities back. Alternatively, intervention could in effect be done by Treasury, with it issuing bills to conduct buybacks and the Fed in turn buying bills in the open market. With this the Fed would be providing funding liquidity that Treasury uses to support market liquidity. A downside is that it could be cumbersome in environments where speed and flexibility are essential. Reserve-management purchases Last December the Fed began reserve-management purchases (RMPs) to rebuild reserves and eventually increase them in line with demand. Any policy measures that result in a smaller or more slowly growing Fed balance sheet would also lessen the need for RMPs, and any shift in the target steady-state Treasury portfolio could alter their composition. Summary While quite speculative at this point, of the ideas outlined above we see most potential for regulatory changes to reduce reserve demand, a shorter-dated Treasury portfolio, and modifications to the structure of market-functioning purchases. It is important to note, though, that while Japan’s ratio of reinvested earnings may seem high, it is not exceptional by global standards. Comparing averages from 2010 to 2024, we find that eurozone countries generally have lower ratios, attributed in part to the low barriers to capital movement within the single currency area. We believe the UK’s low ratio is due to its unique role as an international financial hub, which facilitates capital repatriation and reinvestment. Excluding these specific cases, Japan’s ratio is not notably high, which raises the question of whether the ratio itself is the core issue. The real challenge may lie in Japan's domestic economic environment. From the perspective of rational corporate management, it makes more sense to reinvest profits in lucrative overseas operations or retain foreign-currency-dominated assets as is, given the low level of Japan’s potential growth and interest rates. Consequently, to encourage companies to repatriate these earnings , the government needs to create a more attractive investment climate that will encourage companies to bring their money back to Japan. Without these changes, a large-scale repatriation of funds to Japan is highly unlikely, especially in light of the nation’s inflation-adjusted negative real interest rates. Bottom line: We see the process of balance sheet normalization as a multi-year process, with significant coordination required between the Fed and the Treasury. Given Warsh's stated desire to shrink the balance sheet, and the fact that the Fed's and Treasury's goals need not always be in sync, investors are likely to demand a risk premium during the transition process. What does it mean for markets? Higher repo risk premium: Within the bounds of the "ample" reserves framework, a Warsh- chaired Fed does tip risks somewhat toward higher repo volatility, in our view. Forward ZCIS changes on January CPI releases Source: Barclays Research Watch what you watch: consensus CPI edition What are consensus expectations going into the January CPI print? At face value, this should be easy enough to answer by pulling up the ECO US <GO> screen on Bloomberg (or something similar). However, there are moments when details matter, and this may be one of those months. Specifically, we track that the January fixing, at 325.49, corresponds to a market-implied core at a weak 0.4% m/m (36bp). The Bloomberg consensus CPI NSA forecast is 325.514, very slightly above the fixing, and thus consistent with a c.37bp core, ie, rounding to a 0.4% m/m. This is inconsistent with the median Bloomberg core CPI m/m forecast of 0.3%. As for what is going on here, this could potentially be reflective of different food/energy assumptions, but we offer another potential explanation: differing samples. Indeed, there are only 12 submissions for the CPI NSA consensus, but 66 estimates for the core CPI m/m. As a result, figuring out which represents true 'consensus' becomes more art than science. Put another way: if core prints at 0.30% m/m, is that in line with consensus, or a downside surprise? Similarly, if core prints at 0.37% m/m (rounding to 0.4%), is that an upside surprise? SNB outlook: Policy rate at 0%, despite latest CHF appreciation Recent weeks' CHF appreciation amid geopolitical risks and broader USD weakness has drawn attention and reignited the discussion about SNB FX intervention and/or the risk for negative policy rates. We continue to believe that these developments are insufficient to materially alter the SNB outlook. Our baseline view remains an unchanged policy rate of 0% in 2026 and discretionary FX interventions as first line of defence against CHF strength. This view is based on the SNB's assessment that the policy stance is already expansionary and negative rates are not needed in light of the elevated rate differential to other major economies. It is reinforced by the high hurdle for another rate cut into negative territory that the SNB set after its last rate cut in June. However, if negative rates were coming, we would expect them to be part of a larger rate cut and broader overhaul of the SNB's policy setting, presumably with little guidance or warning. records.text: We attribute the difference in FX returns over the two periods primarily to the fact that, in contrast to the “Deepseek” episode, last week’s sell-off did not prompt a clear “US vs rest-of world” shift. Our US portfolio strategy team notes that last week’s sell-off represented a rotation within the US equity market rather than a broader pull-back, evidenced by the fact that some cyclical pockets of the US equity market saw continued outperformance. While the “Deepseek” episode represented a potential shift in the global beneficiaries of AI from the US to the rest of the world, the recent software sell-off reflects more of a transfer of value within the equity market. Whereas the former had clear implications for future relative asset performance and growth prospects—and therefore a clearer negative impulse for the Dollar—the latter is less clearly a US-specific negative shock. In line with this view, during the “Deepseek” episode, Chinese equities rallied as US equities underperformed, offering investors a clear alternative to US assets (Exhibit 2). In contrast, during the recent software sell-off, Chinese equities fell alongside US equities, and any US underperformance was far more limited than in early 2025, when the shock was more clearly US-negative (Exhibit 3). Morgan Economics has attempted to fill this gap by producing a man- ufacturing expectations index (MEI) for 25 countries, draw- ing on a comprehensive set of PMI future output readings and a wide range of national surveys. Our global aggregate extends back to 2000. We also construct a global service sec- tor expectations index (SEI), but coverage of emerging mar- ket economies is limited. Because of these limitations, our composite expectations index (CEI) is available for a smaller set of economies and begins only in 2012. A simple model of business capex and employment shows that the MEI and CEI have an independent impact on activity (Table 1). Not surprisingly, profits and interest rates have had an impact on global spending and hiring over the past quarter century. After controlling for these key inputs, a 1-standard deviation increase in our manufacturing expectations index (MEI) leads to a 4.3%ar jump in capex and a 0.8%ar rise in employment. The same model estimate from 2012 onward using our CEI shows a more modest but still significant senti- ment impact. • 2025 resilience and imbalance a result of multiple behavioral impulses • Tech optimism and consumer smoothing offset a senti- ment slide that weighed on non-tech business spending • Business caution, rather than AI displacement, pri- marily explains last year’s employment stall • Strong 2H25 growth and easing trade war concerns

records.text: 13 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 14 Deutsche Bank AG Euroland Strategy GBP Rates: Assessing the impact of political uncertainty In the UK. news reports on potential leadership challenges, and shifts in prediction market odds have been dominating discussions over the past week. In this note, we assess how markets have reacted to the news using a PCA-based approach. This suggests swap spreads appear vulnerable to a rise in uncertainty, while in contrast, 5s10s term premium has scope to fall if prediction market odds decline. We develop a framework extracting a UK factor from a PCA analysis using five different UK specific variables. 1) The ratio of FTSE 250/FTSE 100, 2) trade-weighted GBP, 3) difference of GBP 5s10s TP vs EUR/USD, 4) 10Y UK-US ASW differential, and 5) EURGBP fx vol The first factor should capture policy risks specific to the UK, which we then use to assess how a range of GBP rates variables have performed in reaction to the political news. The results are intuitive, and aligns with shifts in prediction market odds. The latter is more difficult to work with given limited history. It correlates most with term premium and swap spreads which are our preferred metrics for fiscal risk. The sell-off in Gilts since the prediction market odds of a new prime minister rose materially has been primarily driven by higher term premia and swap spreads. Change in consumption level during tax-cut period (conceptual diagram for illustration) Source: Barclays Research However, in contrast to real GDP , nominal GDP is likely to decline during the tax‑cut period. This is because the downward impact on the GDP deflator from lower tax‑inclusive prices is likely to outweigh the increase in real GDP . Conversely, nominal GDP is expected to rise when the tax cut ends. In fact, under the uniform consumption tax hike scenario in the Cabinet Office Macroeconomic Model (2022 edition), nominal GDP rises when the tax is increased (and falls when it is cut). In this simulation, we apply the Cabinet Office’s multipliers and assume that nominal GDP declines during the tax‑cut period and rises once the tax cut expires. That said, because food – an essential good – has low price elasticity of demand, the real GDP‑boosting effect of the tax cut itself may be limited in practice. In addition, increases in pre‑tax prices could further reduce the decline in tax‑inclusive prices, dampening the overall effect. Third, the property market has cooled unmistakably, removing what had been a key argument for further tightening. Ultimately, policy-rate adjustments cannot influence the primary driver of Taiwan's current growth upswing-external demand, particularly the tech cycle. With no signs of domestic overheating, we expect the CBC to prioritize conditions in the domestic demand environment rather than respond mechanically to headline growth momentum in 2026. That said, a meaningful surprise in inflation or a renewed shift in real-estate conditions could push the CBC toward a more hawkish stance. Indeed, in 4Q26-1Q27, there is a rising probability that core inflation edges closer to 2%, which could bring the CBC incrementally nearer to considering a rate hike. Therefore, we now expect two 12.5bp rate hikes in 1H27. records.text: On the manufacturing side, forward-looking indicators of output, including the new orders and expectations indices, have moved up in line with (or even more than) the output index, suggesting near-term firmness in activity. Despite softer alternative surveys, our statistical model points to a broadly sideways move in the output index in February (Exhibit 9, left). Similarly, on the services side, the improvement in PMIs has been quite consistent across spot and forward-looking indicators of output, supported by a gradual rise in consumer confidence back towards its long-run mean. Again, given this fairly broad-based improvement, our statistical models suggest that the current expansionary level of activity – as captured by PMIs – is sustainable in the near term and thus predict a broadly sideways move in the headline services index (Exhibit 9, right). Against this broadly positive sentiment backdrop, employment components remain weak. The composite employment index currently stands at 45.8, or 7.9pt below the composite output index level, confirming the negative signal from hard data. The gap between composite output is now the widest observed this cycle and close to its historical records (Exhibit 10), and poses downside risks to the output components of the PMI survey. records.text: Looking ahead, we highlight the following. First, with implieds close to their cycle lows, short volatility positions are not attractive on valuations. Given the increased risk-off dynamics in AI and tech stocks, buying tail risk protection appears to be prudent. Indeed, as we had highlighted a few weeks ago, volatility skew (both calls and puts) has increased sharply over the past few weeks and is likely to remain so. This dynamic will likely keep implieds sticky with the risk of short-term pops higher. Second, delivered volatility is likely to stay muted and well below implieds, which should still be supportive of short gamma positions. Against this backdrop, we favour short-gamma/long vega strategies. In Figure 18W e f a v o u r s h o r t g a m m a / l o n g - v e g a e x p o s u r e v i a s y n t h e t i c f o r w a r d v o l a t i l i t y s t r u c t u r e s , we pres- ent a list of synthetic forward volatility structures, constructed using a triangle of swaption straddles, which are short-gamma/long-vega at inception. records.text: uling coalition’s landslide victory in the lower house election, fiscal concerns have receded, and markets have increasingly priced in an acceleration of the BoJ’s rate‑hiking cycle. In this context, uncertainty surrounding the terminal rate, as reflected in the OIS term premium, has instead declined. This trend is also evident in the swaption market. The probability distribution of the terminal rate pricing derived from 2y forward 3m swaptions had shown a rightward shift (higher rate expectations) and a wider dispersion (greater uncertainty) since late November, but these movements have largely stalled as markets increasingly priced in a landslide LDP victory in the election ( Figure 10). Looking ahead, we expect developments to be driven less by term premiums and more by increases in the risk‑neutral yield as BoJ rate hikes actually materialize. We have brought forward our expected timing of BoJ rate hikes and raised our terminal rate forecast from 1.25% to 1.50%. While this revision alone would push the 10y risk‑neutral yield (RNY) up by roughly 20bp, we have also taken into account offsetting downward pressures from a pullback in fiscal concerns and terminal rate uncertainty. As a result, we have raised our 10y yield forecast by 15bp in this update. 13 February 2026 19 Barclays | Market Strategy Japan: Post-election outlook for policy and yen rates

records.text: Global Macro Strategy - Views and Trade Ideas 13 February 2026 Citi Research 13 A closer look at the structural bid for CHF. For reasons outlined in detail by the SNB (23 Nov 2017), Switzerland has a persistent current account surplus that does not get fully recycled by private investor outflows (Figure 22). As such, the SNB historically helps to balance this by increasing its FX reserves in line with the accumulated current account surplus (Figure 23). One implication of this is that domestic FX policy is highly relevant for CHF, and while the relationship is a noisy one, we do observe that under- and over-accumulation of FX reserves relative to the growth in the current account surplus can lead to sustained rallies and sell-offs in CHF (Figure 24). Source: Citi Research Source: Citi Research Just as a reminder, the premise of the systematic short vol strategy is that investors are willing to pay more for options with higher implied volatility as insurance against unexpected market moves, hence the extra cost known as the risk premium. By shorting the straddle options, the seller is counting on the actual market movement to be less than what the swaption market expects and the profit is the difference between the premium collected and the realized payout . For the analysis, we systematically sell a 1m10y ATMF straddle on each business day and hold the position until the swaption’s expiry. After the initial month, we essentially have a short portfolio of around twenty 1m10y straddles with each scheduled to expire one after the other and a new straddle sold daily as replacement . We run the backtesting analysis going back more than 20 years starting from 2004 to present . Selling straddles when implied vol is low has historically been the most profitable. Not surprising, shorting vol in general has been historically profitable, and this is why it has consistently been a popular strategy. But we don’t expect the data to be weak enough to support a back-to-back cut in March and April. In our view, the BoE would need to see a marked deterioration in growth and labour data to deliver back to back cuts, particularly given its need for more evidence as policy approaches neutral. We don’t expect that in upcoming prints. Meanwhile political uncertainty around an immediate leadership challenge to PM Starmer subsided this week. We continue to think that post May local elections is when risks of a leadership challenge to the PM could rise. If a leadership challenge were to occur, the nature of the Labour leadership election process and potential negative market reaction to any suggestion of fiscal laxity, imply to us that a new Labour leader or breaking the fiscal rules are not foregone conclusions. This would be consistent with year-on-year core inflation around ~2.7/2.8% in H1, before falling back towards 2.4/2.5% in 2027 (Figure 7). While our forecasts for H2 are slightly higher, as discussed below, with the Supreme Court ruling on IEEPA tariffs remaining a downside risk, we maintain a neutral view on the front-end. records.text: 13 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 61 is already more generous regarding the required minimum OC for 10% risk weighted CB. Moreover, the EC LCR Delegated Act already allows a LCR level 1 eligibility for CB, with BIS still recommending level 2A eligibility at best. Overall, the question seems how much further regulatory support the EU wants to provide to its CB market, which has a record large outstanding volume already. Estimating capital relief for EEA banks - challenging but substantial The total global outstanding volume of CB has grown from approximately EUR 1.7tn equivalent in 2007 to likely over EUR 3.35tn in Feb 2026. In case the proposed 5% RW would become effective, it will likely only apply to EU Premium CB. EEA CB account for a maximum of 85% of the global CB market, i.e. roughly EUR 2850bn equivalent. records.text: 13 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 5 If the Fed retains ample reserves, as we learned from funding market pressures observed late last year, it cannot let reserves fall from current levels without risking significant upward pressure on the fed funds rate. That is, unless it can reduce bank demand for reserves. The path to lower reserves demand would come primarily via regulatory changes. Two options that come to mind would be relaxing the liquidity coverage ratio or internal liquidity stress test requirements so that banks demand fewer cash assets. In line with this train of thought, Governors Bowman and Miran have recently argued that the Fed’s balance sheet is “downstream of bank regulations.” We expect to hear more on this theme in coming months. The Fed could also reduce total assets without lowering reserves if its other liabilities were to decline. To this end, while currency can be thought of as exogenously determined, Treasury could run a lower TGA balance or the Fed could restrict or disincentivize usage of the foreign repo pool (i.e., ONRRP for foreign central banks), which has a current balance of around $320bn. Reducing securities holdings For a given level of total assets, the Fed’s securities portfolio could be reduced. This would most likely entail using repo. First, the perception of risk remains high (even before challenges to EU cohesion in regards to Greenland). Second, the SAFE programme for defense spending loans was oversubscribed. The latest CBI Retail Sales measure also jumped 27pts to -17. Renewed discounting post-Christmas, we think, will also push spending. Our models point to a 0.9% m-o-m rise in retail spending volumes taking the annual rate up to 4.3%. Public Finances: The January report will be a very important one to keep an eye on - given how important it is to overall tax receipts. January tends to be the largest month for cash and accrued tax receipts, accounting for balancing payments on the previous year's self-assessment income tax and capital gains tax. Higher PAYE income and NICs accounting for Christmas bonuses also tend to feed through into January tax receipts, with VAT receipts following Christmas sales also boosting revenues. To be sure though, this report likely won't be incorporated by the OBR with the Spring Statement now less than three weeks away. Nevertheless, it will be an important marker to gauge the trajectory of the public finances. What are we expecting for January? Debt servicing costs, we expect, will undershoot the OBR's estimate. We expect receipts to remain stronger than projected too - on the back of still healthy pay growth and corporation tax receipts. records.text: Japan FX and Rates Strategy Yen-rates forecast update based on stabilization in risk premium We update our yen-rates forecast with risk premium stabilizing on the LDP election landslide and faster BoJ hikes. FY26 JGB flow-based supply-demand is set to deteriorate for sub-10y sector while improving in superlongs, but the 10-25y is likely to see sharp deterioration on a stock basis. Rates Strategy Shinichiro Kadota BSJL, Japan | Ayao Ehara BSJL, Japan This week: LDP landslide victory drives a sharp decline in superlong term premium This week saw a sharp twist-flattening led by the superlong sector after the LDP’s landslide victory in the lower house election on the 8th (see LDP landslide victory to stabilize risk premium, 9 February). As the LDP’s strong showing had already been widely anticipated ahead of the election, yields in the superlong sector had declined to some extent by the end of last week, but buying accelerated further at the start of this week. By contrast, uncertainty surrounding the timing of the BoJ’s next rate hike remains elevated. The Nikkei reported on the 10th that the US-Japan summit could add pressure for a rate hike at the March BoJ meeting, leading to bear-flattening pressure out to the long-term sector. Meanwhile, the JGBi 10y auction held on the 10th turned out in line with our expectations. records.text: US Rates Weekly 13 February 2026 Citi Research 4 Overview: Longing for the front-end Jobs seasonality and equity/UST connection are bullish The return of USTs/equities correlation increases our conviction in receiving 1y2y SOFR (entered in US Rates Weekly - The Foxy Five – 2026 Edition). The AI backdrop brings a strong disinflation narrative with it, where USTs should be more responsive to risk-off moves. Presumably, increased AI disruption increases volatility around future job prints. The simple fact is if the AI bubble bursts or if it induces risk-offs via disruption, at some point later this year front-end yields will move lower. Put succinctly, the market can price in a lower neutral rate as 2026 plays out. T o be clear, last week's UST rally, on the back of the equity sell-off, was easier to understand since weaker jobs data implies a higher chance for rate cuts. Still, we think the market’s view of ‘neutral’ will keep shifting lower, especially in light of today’s CPI which again shows shelter will anchor core CPI towards 2% by year- end. Treasuries brushed off the strong headline NFP print with the front-end of the curve, led by early 2027 Fed pricing, leading the way (Figure 4). Our 5s30s curve steepener was performing well until yesterday’s very strong 30y auction, although steepening picked back up after today’s tepid inflation print. records.text: However, monthly prices are showing early signs of retracement which should send greater urgency to policymakers to be proactive in 2026 as opposed to be reactive in 2025. As China continues to rely on SMPI for targeted stimulus, we do not anticipate Chinese yields to compress given the lack of liquidity injection. This is not to say that the PBoC will reduce their share of CGBs as total bond issuance in 2026 should be even higher than last year’s CNY13.9trn. However, the recent resumption of CGB trading by the PBoC should be viewed in the context of keeping a stable yield curve and offsetting any foreign selling as opposed to easing aggregate monetary policy (Figure 10). All-in-all, internal headwinds remain but investor sentiment has greatly improved as we anticipate further rotation out of Chinese bonds into equities while CNY should be well anchored with an upward bias against the USD. Indeed, the January print has come out above the market fixing in ten out of the past eleven years (2021 being the exception; Figure 8), with an average (median) beat of 14bp (16bp). Concerning economic data, the market has recently traded as if risks were shifting to the downside, with short-end real yields rallying and forward inflation (such as 1y1y and 2y1y) falling, at least before the January labour market report. This is somewhat at odds with data surprise indicators, which have risen this year (Figure 9). A solid labour market report should alleviate these concerns, and with GDP growth running at above -trend levels, labour markets (and indicators of slack such as the quits rate) showing signs of stabilisation, and the fiscal and monetary impulse expected to be positive this year, the economic backdrop should be supportive for inflation markets. Tariffs add to the medium -term uncertainty, and the Supreme Court ruling on IEEPA remains a downside risk for front -end inflation, with betting markets currently seeing a close to ~75% chance of a decision against ( Figure 10). records.text: 13 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG Fixed Income Blogs What could Warsh mean for the Fed’s balance sheet? Introduction A prior note discussed the potential implications of Kevin Warsh’s nomination as Fed chair. It highlighted his critiques of Fed policy and claims that a smaller Fed balance sheet could reduce inflation and allow for lower policy rates. Here we consider various ways the Fed could plausibly achieve a smaller or less active balance sheet or securities portfolio, or one with less duration risk, as well as related considerations. In doing so, we separately discuss the current balance sheet, both size and composition, and potential future asset purchases. Overall, we see the most likely path to a smaller balance sheet as coming through regulatory changes that reduce bank reserves demand, though adjustments to the Fed’s ample reserve regime could also allow for a smaller securities portfolio. With respect to portfolio composition, the Fed is reducing its MBS holdings and could speed that process with sales. The Committee has not yet settled on a target steady- state Treasury portfolio and we see reasonable prospects that under Warsh it could choose one that is significantly shorter-dated than the universe outstanding. On future QE, we find it very unlikely that the Committee would forfeit an effective tool of monetary policy at the zero lower bound but could envision a different structure for purchases to address market dysfunction. records.text: 12/02/2026 US equities: A tech crash A powerful tailwind to economic growth: We believe the AI infrastructure buildout was a key factor keeping the US economy out of recession in 2025. Our base case sees continued momentum in investment, while indirect effects on business sentiment and consumer wealth persist (see US: If you build it, AI will come, dated 17 October 2025). Equity crash risks triggering recession: In this ‘grey swan’, GenAI monetization fails to emerge and an equity market crash fans the flames of recession. The bursting of the dot-com bubble triggered a lengthy sell-off from March 2000 to October 2002, which contributed to the 2001 recession. We model a similar 40% drop in equity prices and a 100bp increase in corporate borrowing spreads using NiGEM, a large-scale macroeconomic model. The net result is a 2pp reduction in the level of real GDP and 1pp increase in the unemployment rate, both of which would be consistent with recession. An additional risk is that the climb out of a downturn could be weaker than normal, as fiscal firepower is limited and firms are increasingly seeking out ways to use AI tools in lieu of adding workers. Imported inflation is a barometer for the pass-through of CHF moves but does likely not yet reflect much of the CHF appreciation of recent weeks. The TWI appreciation since the beginning of the year - if maintained - could lower inflation by 0.1-0.2pp and thus bring it to or below zero, according to our estimates. However, we work with a time horizon of one to two quarters for the FX pass-through to core inflation, so the lack of impact in the January data is not surprising. February could show a bigger effect on energy inflation (via oil prices), while the full pass-through will likely take longer. Inflation to remain subdued in 2026 After 0.2% average annual inflation in 2025, we expect only a very modest pickup to 0.3% in 2026. records.text: Our estimates imply that a single hawkish dissenter in a ten-member committee raises expected policy at the following meeting by 4bp. However, this effect falls to around 2bp if dissents had also been observed at the prior meeting, suggesting that the dissent signal for future policy outcomes is weaker if voters have established a pattern of serial dissenting. We find the effects to be similar regardless of if the dissent was made in favor of a hold or a policy change. Financial markets react in manners directionally consistent with the policy signal from dissents shown above. In Exhibit 5, we regress the daily move in expected short rates over the year ahead and equities on the meeting date on our dissent spread measure. We control for the policy rate change at the meeting to isolate the incremental effect of the dissent signal. A hawkish dissent by a quarter of the committee is associated with a 0.7bp rise in expected short rates and an 8bp decrease in daily equity returns. While these effects are small and likely affected by the degree of surprise of the dissent, they affirm that market expectations are informed by the degree of consensus of the committee. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 13 February 2026 3 The market view on France seems to have zoomed in on budget negotiations and perhaps soon the 2027 election, but the macro actually shows potential for particularly one-sided risks. More in our main piece this week. Euro area wage tracker: stuck below 3% While we are on the theme of disinflation, our view remains that the Euro area will also undershoot the 2% target (just not as much as France). This week’s ECB wage tracker update has not challenged that view. 2026 wage growth appears on track for less growth than last year across different measures. All of them point to sub-3% negotiated wage growth. Headline at 2.4% for 2026 is now only 20bp above the 2013-24 average – hardly a comfortable place. True, the year is still young and the wage tracker for 2Q-4Q26 currently reflects c 30% of employees only, vs close to 50% in 2025. New deals may look better. Then again, it’s exactly in France where most of new info to still come (wage tracker currently at c 20% vs 50% of employee coverage last year). And, if our disinflation view is right on France, these deals are unlikely to move the Euro area tracker higher. UK: data to support gradual cuts Data next week should show inflation slow down to 3.0%, private pay growth slow to 3.4%, weak hiring and unemployment flat at 5.1%. records.text: Oil Monitor 11 February 2026 Citi Research 2 As our short-term price target of $70/bbl being met but Iranian tensions continue to simmer, we mark-to-market our 1Q’26 Brent average to $67 and 1Q’26 WTI to $64. Developments in US RINs and Biofuels In mid-January, Reuters reported on the EPA’s proposed ruling to increase Renewable Volume Obligations (RVO) meaningfully in 2026 and 2027. The expectation is that the agency will finalize the ruling in the next few weeks and share it with the White House for approval (Reuters, 01/15/2026). The main driver for higher RVOs is driven by meaningfully higher biomass-based diesel (BBD) and advanced biofuel RVOs. Higher D4 RINs prices, representing a greater incentive to produce renewable diesel and biodiesel, would also be bullish for corresponding feedstocks, notably soybean oil. RINs price moves would be mirrored by the spread between biodiesel and ULSD prices, as well as soybean oil and ULSD prices (BO- HO spread). We reviewed the original ruling that was first released in June and supplement proposal released in September here. Besides a sharp increase in RIN prices little has changed since then yet, policy-wise, but markets look to be expecting policy tightening. RIN prices are up 59% in 2026 compared with 2025 averages. The rally in part can be explained by lower RIN generation levels in 2025, which fell by 10% y/y, as biodiesel and renewable diesel generation fell by 45% and 16% y/y, respectively. However, we believe that even if rhetoric based on such policy biases temporarily amplifies market concerns, policy management will ultimately settle into a prudent stance that stabilizes market risk premia, driven by market and external pressures (see LDP landslide victory to stabilize risk premium, 9 February). In fact, PM Takaichi initially emphasized resistance to BoJ rate hikes and aggressive fiscal policy following the LDP presidential election last October, but only two months later in December, she tolerated additional BoJ hikes. Swap spreads have been catching up and taken together this is consistent with more fiscal risk being priced. At the time of writing, there are three main conclusions. Firstly 5s10s term premium is in line levels implied by the first factor, while 10s30s term premium appears marginally too low. Secondly, swap spreads appear rich. This likely reflects expectations of regulatory reform that reduce bank balance sheet constraints which we had also expected to contribute to spread performance. Overall, the ability of spreads to rely on these factors has likely reached its limits, and it seems reasonable to think that a continued rise in prediction market odds will also drag on spreads from here. As such, we close out our 10y asw recommendation; even if the newsflow has calmed down, it is unlikely that the perception of fiscal risk is going to fully dissipate. Where do we go from Keir?: While the catalyst may differ, the process for a change in leadership, whether it is through a resignation or a challenge, is broadly the same. In both scenarios, the process spans several weeks (likely six to eight weeks), with the primary difference being that in a leadership challenge the sitting prime minister is automatically included on the ballot. There are two stages to a leadership contest: the nomination and the ballot. ▪ Nomination: Candidates must be nominated by at least 20% of Labour MPs (slightly over 80 MPs). They must then be endorsed by either 5% of constituency- level Labour parties or three party affiliates (at least two unions), whose combined members should amount to at least 5% of affiliated membership. ▪ Ballot: Nominated candidates will be put on a ranked choice ballot for eligible Labour Party members and affiliates. Though official figures for 2026 have not yet been confirmed, reports indicate that the party’s membership has declined drastically over the last few years and has shifted further to the centre as members have defected to the Greens and other parties. Following the ballot process, the first candidate to receive more than 50% of the vote share will become the new leader of the Labour Party and the prime minister. mption dynamics emerges. The productivity surge is also consistent with the observed decoupling between the labor market and the demand side of the economy. The question remains on how sustainable is this current dynamic and how this imbalance will correct over time. As we have discussed extensively, we expect the labor market to recover in line with the robustness of aggregate spending rather than consumption slowing down in line with the weakness in the labor market. In other words, we see the labor market as a lagging rather than a leading indicator of the health of the economy. Is labor really responsible for the improvements in productity? The observed increase in productivity, which is by construction assigned to labor, coupled with the surge in the fraction of national income going to profits of companies, begs the question on whether these are real improvements in labor productivity. Unfortunately, there is not enough data yet to answer that question, but anecdotal evidence seems to point towards a more marked increase in the marginal product of capital rather than the marginal product of labor. Time will tell if real wages catch up with real profits. It may have been a lucky coincidence that fiscal policy couldn’t adjust. • We expect a fairly steady growth trajectory. But France is subject to particularly asymmetric downside risks. Holistic disinflation and a questionable policy mix Growth prospects were in the spotlight in our recent focus on Italy and Germany. Inflation (or the lack of) and the policy mix take centre stage in our focus on France today. Disinflation has gone very far in the economy – perhaps too far at this stage. And it is not just a fluke from seasonality, it spreads across price components: Consumer price inflation is well below the Euro area average. Private sector unit profits have corrected lower than the Euro area average, too. And, wage dynamics are below 2019 levels, as well. How come? Monetary policy is likely much too tight for the economy. If the ECB hiking cycle went too far and cuts not far enough for the Euro area (our long-held view), it’s even more extreme in France, where the inflation peak was lower. The policy mix is back. records.text: We would expect yields to rally, with 5y5y term premium compressing by roughly 25bp as growth and spending forecasts are revised downward. German ASWs should richen, and in a risk-off environment the 10-year BTP–Bund spread could widen by 10–15bp. On the back of earnings downgrades and valuations derating, the SX5E and the DAX could fall by double digits (both by around 15%). The resulting bias for ECB rate cuts and weaker growth could push EURUSD toward the 1.15 level. Lower yields, richer German ASW and wider EGB spreads: In a scenario where the market lowers its estimates of future bond issuance and growth expectations, the most exposed across rates would be German yields and ASW, which we would expect to rally. With German bonds leading the moves, EU integration being questioned and equities trading risk-off (see below), EGB spreads should widen. Based on the beta of 10y BTP–Bunds to equities alone, this would point towards a 10–15bp widening of spreads. At the front end, the market should erode the prospect of ECB hikes and price a higher likelihood of rate cuts as growth and inflation expectations are revised lower. Further out on the curve, the pricing out of bond issuance should also exert downside pressure on term premium, worth around 25bp on the 5y5y. Combined, these could leave the curve roughly unchanged near current spot levels. Earnings downgrades and valuations derating: We would expect a pullback of the MEGA theme to see sharp downward revisions in earnings.

records.text: likely entail using repo. One approach could be to use repo to help efficiently run an ample regime, particular amid uncertain shifts in reserve demand, in what some refer to as a “demand-driven floor system.” In this setup, the Fed’s securities portfolio would be sized to leave reserves in structural deficiency, and price-based repo operations would be used to fill the gap. This could shrink the balance sheet by eliminating any excess reserves buffer, but more importantly would substitute repo for Treasuries and MBS and thus lower the Fed’s duration footprint. Other major central banks, such as the BoE, effectively operate various forms of a demand-driven floor system. Another approach would be to use repo operations to sterilize the reserve impact of TGA fluctuations. Here the Fed would roughly match TGA balances with repo, the result of which would be a smaller securities portfolio over time. We first heard of the idea from Bill Nelson, chief economist at BPI; it was subsequently mentioned in Governor Miran’s first speech after joining the Fed. A separate possibility being discussed again is to revalue the Fed’s gold holdings. Revaluation can be thought of as initially boosting the TGA and then, as those balances are drawn down, adding to reserves. For a given reserve-level target, within an ample regime or otherwise, the Fed would ultimately hold fewer securities alongside the revalued gold. records.text: ab 13 February 2026 Global Research European Economic Comment Switzerland: Inflation as expected, for now Inflation unchanged at 0.1% y/y in January Swiss inflation remained unchanged at 0.1% y/y in January (-0.1% m/m), in line with consensus, our estimate, and the SNB's forecast for a Q1 average of 0.1%. Core inflation remained unchanged at 0.5% y/y, in line with our expectation. Looking into the details, the drivers of the unchanged print were broadly as expected, but on the margin, food and goods inflation surprised slightly to the upside and energy and services to the downside. Specifically, energy inflation rose 1pp to -4.3% y/y, partly driven by base effects in the annual electricity price adjustment, where electricity prices declined only 3% this year after the 9% decline in 2025. Yet the increase in energy inflation was smaller than we had forecast, due to downside surprises in fuel and gas prices. Food and goods inflation rose by 0.4pp to -0.4%y/y and -1.3% y/y, respectively - both above our expectation. This was offset by a 0.3pp decline in services inflation to 0.9%. Looking ahead, we track inflation at 0% y/y in February, but flag significant uncertainty from rents (due to the pass-through of the second reference rate decline) and recent CHF appreciation. The outcomes beyond May, absent a large turnaround in polling for Starmer, seem to a political shift leftwards, given Labour politicians are considerably more left-leaning than party voters in the broader population. While Starmer has a majority of MPs in the House of Commons, he does not have a majority within his own party. The blocking majority in his party prefer more spending and are against reducing welfare spending. There are two strong pieces of evidence that the aggregate Labour party is structurally more left-leaning on tax and spending than the party leadership. First, in summer 2025 they rebelled against lowering the welfare bill by 0.33% annually, forcing the bill to be watered down and reducing any savings to nearly 0. Second, in the November budget, MPs pushed a government U-turn, leading them to raise child benefit allowance. This was unpopular across voters from every party. This policy change received support primarily from Labour MPs in recent Parliamentary confirmation votes. records.text: One way some market participants have suggested the Fed could accelerate shifts in its portfolio would be to engage in an asset swap with Treasury, with Treasury taking the Fed’s MBS in exchange for T-bills of equivalent value. This would give Treasury more control over the future of the MBS portfolio, remove duration and spread risk from the Fed’s balance sheet, and arguably better align with the principle that Treasury controls debt management policy. But our understanding is that such an effort would require legislation, not just to raise the debt limit given the needed increase in bills, but also because the Federal Reserve Act requires MBS sales and bill purchases to be done in the open market. Future asset purchases Turning to future purchases, the Fed has historically done QE with two goals: (1) easing the stance of monetary policy by fostering more accommodative financial conditions and (2) resolving dysfunction in core fixed-income markets. We consider these, as well as RMPs, separately. Monetary policy purchases Purchases to ease the stance of monetary policy have only been initiated by the Committee when its policy rate is at zero, which it considers to be the effective lower bound. The staff and Committee have historically viewed QE as an effective tool for easing broad financial conditions by lowering longer-term rates. A final factor to consider is the relationship between hedge ratios and interest rates. Although expensive to hedge when interest rates are high and rising, the pattern of investor behaviour over the past 20 years links higher interest rates in EM with an increasing propensity to hedge. This at first does not make sense, given the expense of hedging when interest rates are high. However, high rates in EM often coincide with crises; either domestic balance of payments or fiscal problems, or as a result of a global economic crash. It is clear that, more than the cost, investors fear more the FX volatility and uncertainty that accompanies periods of high rates (Figure 4). Figure 4 Easing rates should lower HRs Source: State Street Markets The above relationship, however, has broken down over the past year. Trump’s second presidency has added a new source of uncertainty. This is highlighted by the jump in hedge ratios around Liberation Day – a rise that subsequently struggled to reverse. President Trump’s trade wars, it turns out, has not dented the global economic cycle with export figures from Asia point ing to a boom. Perhaps, for that reason, the fear factor, evident in FX hedging, has been reassessed. As a result, the old relationship bet ween hedging activity and EM interest rates has reasserted itself. records.text: Sarah Dong +1(212)357-9741 | sarah.dong@gs.com Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC Global Economics Comment: Canary on the Committee? 12 February 2026 | 12:58PM EST Most major central banks make policy rate decisions by committee and reveal n voting outcomes, but the extent of open disagreement varies greatly by central bank. Since 2022, there has been at least one dissent at every BoE meeting, but at less than 10% of Riksbank meetings. In this Global Economics Comment, we document the sources of, and signals from, monetary policy dissents. Using the historical voting records of ten global central banks, we find that n dissents are less common when unemployment is undershooting trend but more common following changes in inflation and increases in unemployment over trend, suggesting that central bankers are typically united in heeding the message from a weaker labor market but disagree more often about whether inflation is transitory or persistent. In addition, dissents are persistent meeting-to-meeting but tend to decline following leadership changes. We also find that dissents predict future policy moves. A hawkish dissent from n 10% of the committee (e.g. a single dissenter in a ten-member committee) predicts a 4bp increase in the policy rate at the next meeting. However, the signal decays when voters dissent at consecutive meetings, implying that dissents are less predictive of future policy when voters have established views that differ from the committee consensus. We have seen early signs of a broadening out in manufacturing activity. • Broader investment should contribute to better labor demand this year and improve the foundation of the economic expansion. Complete report: US Economic Weekly: Investment is not just an AI story in 2026 13 February 2026 AI investment isn’t going anywhere yet AI related investment was a big story in 2025. It contributed to the acceleration seen in investment in computers and peripheral equipment, software, data centers, and research and development. Together these categories contributed an average of 0.9pp to GDP growth through the first three quarters of 2025 (Exhibit 1). Meanwhile, all other nonresidential investment had little effect on growth over the same period. To be sure not all of investment in these categories can be chalked up to AI. Also, much of the equipment category is imported. Therefore, the role AI investment played in growth is much smaller than what the investment numbers suggest. Still, AI was a big factor in last year’s surprisingly resilient investment data as fiscal stimulus for green energy and semiconductors faded.
